articles.title: UP govt renames Noida International Airport after PM
articles.summary: UP cabinet renames Noida International Airport to Narendra Modi International Airport, Noida-Jewar; IATA code DXN unchanged, branding updates needed.
articles.body: Noida: Nearly four months after flight operations began from Noida International Airport, the state cabinet on Friday renamed it Narendra Modi International Airport, Noida-Jewar. Chief minister Yogi Adityanath said the decision was taken to mark the completion of 25 years of the PM’s public life.While the renaming will not affect the airport’s IATA code DXN, it will require changes to official name displays, branding and booking-related information.“Noida International Airport is a major gift to UP from the PM. In the coming years, this airport will take the state’s economy, industry, tourism and global connectivity to new heights. With this very sentiment, the cabinet has passed the proposal,” the CM said.Yogi also credited the PM for UP’s industrial growth, its development as a major IT hub and the expansion of social welfare schemes to cover crores of beneficiaries. He said under Prime Minister’s leadership and guidance, the state govt will continue working with full energy, sincerity and commitment to realise the resolve of ‘Viksit Uttar Pradesh, Viksit Bharat-2047’.Referring to Modi’s links with UP, the CM said the PM was an elected representative from Kashi. He recalled the PM’s 2014 visit to Kashi, when he had said that “Maa Ganga has called me”. Since then, he said, the relationship between Kashi and the PM had gone beyond political representation, with a new bond emerging between the development of Kashi, its spiritual renaissance and the overall development of UP.PM completed 25 years as the head of a govt on Oct 7, beginning with his tenure as Gujarat chief minister in 2001. “This is a glorious chapter in Indian democratic history. This 25-year journey has been guided by the spirit of service, dedication and nation first,” Yogi said.Jewar MLA Dhirendra Singh said renaming the airport “is a tribute to the visionary leadership that has transformed Jewar from a predominantly rural region into an emerging global aviation and industrial destination”.While Noida International Airport did not comment on the issue, Yamuna Authority and Noida International Airport Limited CEO RK Singh said they will ensure compliance with govt order.The foundation stone of the airport, developed by Yamuna International Airport Private Limited, a subsidiary of Swiss firm Zurich Airport International AG, was laid by PM on Nov 25, 2021, and domestic flight operations began on June 15 this year after he inaugurated it. articles.title: Mensagens sexuais no Teams levam funcionária à justa causa | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisão da Justiça do Trabalho em Osasco considerou a troca recorrente de mensagens durante o expediente; funcionária questionou o monitoramento das conversas pela empresa.
articles.summary: Decisão da Justiça do Trabalho em Osasco considerou a troca recorrente de mensagens durante o expediente; funcionária questionou o monitoramento das conversas pela empresa.
articles.body:
Funcionária é demitida por justa causa após trocar mensagens sexuais com colegas pelo Teams — Foto: Pexels

Uma funcionária que usava o Microsoft Teams da empresa para manter conversas pessoais e de teor sexual com colegas de trabalho teve a demissão por justa causa mantida pela Justiça do Trabalho.

A decisão é da 5ª Vara do Trabalho de Osasco, na Grande São Paulo, e chama atenção por envolver o uso recorrente de uma ferramenta corporativa para assuntos sem relação com o trabalho.

Segundo o processo, as mensagens eram trocadas durante o expediente e incluíam referências a encontros íntimos que ocorreriam no horário de trabalho e até mesmo dentro das dependências da empresa .

Ao analisar o caso, a Justiça concluiu que o problema não estava na vida privada da empregada nem no relacionamento amoroso que ela mantinha com outro funcionário. O que pesou foi a forma como questões pessoais foram levadas para o ambiente profissional de maneira frequente e prolongada.

De acordo com a decisão, a empresa aplicou a justa causa após identificar que a trabalhadora utilizava repetidamente a plataforma corporativa de comunicação interna para tratar de assuntos particulares.

Em audiência, a funcionária admitiu que mantinha um relacionamento íntimo com outro empregado da companhia e reconheceu que pode ter trocado mensagens de conteúdo sexual com ele e também com outros colegas .

Ela também confirmou a autenticidade de capturas de tela apresentadas pela empresa como prova no processo.

Para a juíza Cristiane Serpa Panzan, a própria admissão da autora reforçou a validade do material anexado aos autos e eliminou dúvidas sobre quem enviou as mensagens.

Na avaliação da magistrada, não se tratava de um episódio isolado ou de um uso eventual da ferramenta para tratar de questões pessoais. As conversas teriam ocorrido de forma reiterada ao longo de vários meses.

Ao tentar reverter a demissão, a trabalhadora argumentou que as provas seriam ilegais porque resultaram do monitoramento das comunicações realizadas pela plataforma corporativa.

A empresa, por sua vez, apresentou normas internas que regulamentavam o uso dos sistemas de trabalho e informavam aos empregados sobre a possibilidade de monitoramento das comunicações realizadas por meio dessas ferramentas .

A juíza rejeitou o argumento da funcionária. Na sentença, afirmou que o acompanhamento das mensagens, dentro dos limites previstos pelas regras internas, faz parte do poder de fiscalização do empregador e não representa, por si só, violação à privacidade do trabalhador .

Segundo a magistrada, a própria jurisprudência trabalhista admite esse tipo de controle quando realizado em sistemas corporativos.

A decisão destaca que a gravidade da conduta não decorreu apenas do teor sexual das mensagens.

Para a Justiça, a conclusão foi baseada em um conjunto de fatores:

uso de uma ferramenta corporativa para fins alheios ao trabalho;

conversas realizadas durante a jornada de trabalho;

conteúdo sem relação com as atividades profissionais;

referências a encontros íntimos durante o expediente e nas dependências da companhia.

A juíza entendeu que a situação ultrapassou um simples desvio ocasional e configurou falta grave suficiente para enquadrar a conduta como mau procedimento e ato de indisciplina.

Com isso, o pedido para transformar a justa causa em demissão sem justa causa foi negado.

⚠️ Apesar da derrota na primeira instância, o caso ainda não está encerrado . O processo segue pendente de análise de recurso e poderá ser reavaliado pelas instâncias superiores da Justiça do Trabalho.

articles.title: Ambulância de prefeitura é vista fazendo entrega de encomendas no ES | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-entregadora se surpreendeu ao devolver mercadorias e se deparar com veículo da Prefeitura de Pancas na porta da casa dela.
articles.summary: Ex-entregadora se surpreendeu ao devolver mercadorias e se deparar com veículo da Prefeitura de Pancas na porta da casa dela.
articles.body:
Uma ambulância da Prefeitura de Pancas , no Noroeste do Espírito Santo, foi flagrada recolhendo encomendas na casa de uma ex-entregadora de plataformas de vendas on-line. O caso aconteceu na segunda-feira (5) e foi registrado em vídeo pela mulher, que se surpreendeu ao ver o veículo no local.

A ex-entregadora, que preferiu não se identificar, contou que trabalhava com a entrega de mercadorias no município e em cidades da região, mas decidiu devolver os pacotes após um desentendimento relacionado a um pedido perdido.

Segundo ela, a responsável pelas entregas enviou outra pessoa para buscar as encomendas. Ao tentar fazer a devolução, no entanto, a ex-entregadora se deparou com uma ambulância do município.

Confusa por não ter acionado ambulância nenhuma, ela disse ter demorado a compreender que o veículo estava ali por causa das mercadorias.

A mulher gravou o momento em que os pacotes foram recolhidos e enviou o vídeo à coordenação do posto de saúde da cidade. A coordenadora confirmou ter enviado o veículo para buscar as encomendas e reclamou da gravação depois que as imagens repercutiram nas redes sociais.

Em nota publicada nas redes sociais, a Secretaria Municipal de Saúde da Prefeitura de Pancas informou que determinou a abertura de uma sindicância para apurar o caso e identificar possíveis responsáveis.

articles.title: Mulher comemora divórcio com espumante e música na saída de cartório | G1
articles.standfirst: Anielle Santana Silva, de 38 anos, celebrou o divórcio como forma de ressignificar o fim de um ciclo e marcar um recomeço. A história foi registrada em Araguaína, no norte do Tocantins.
articles.summary: Anielle Santana Silva, de 38 anos, celebrou o divórcio como forma de ressignificar o fim de um ciclo e marcar um recomeço. A história foi registrada em Araguaína, no norte do Tocan
articles.body:
A enfermeira Anielle Santana Silva, de 38 anos, comemorou seu divórcio com espumante e música na saída de um cartório em Araguaína , região norte do Tocantins. A nova fase foi celebrada com um grupo de quatro amigas.

📱 Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 TO no WhatsApp

O momento foi publicado nesta sexta-feira (9) e viralizou nas redes sociais, com quase 100 mil visualizações. Anielle surge caminhando na calçada com o documento de divórcio em mãos enquanto as amigas a aguardam segurando taças.

"Por trás daquele sorriso existe uma mulher que precisou reunir forças para escolher a si mesma, mesmo diante dos medos e das incertezas", conta Anielle.

Recepcionada ao som de uma música da dupla Zé Neto & Cristiano, a enfermeira é recebida pelas amigas, que ironizam a situação com o trecho da letra: "Achei que ia durar pra sempre, tô triste com um negócio desse, escuta aí o barulho do foguete". Em seguida, elas estouram confetes coloridos para o alto.

Anielle Santana (à esq) com as amigas — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Em conversa com o g1 , ela explica que a celebração não é uma forma de debochar da situação, mas uma maneira de ressignificar o processo de separação e comemorar os recomeços.

"A minha comemoração não foi por uma derrota, nem por desejar o mal a alguém, mas pela sensação de liberdade, coragem de recomeçar e esperança de viver uma nova fase com mais paz, leveza e felicidade", explica.

A enfermeira afirma que a ideia de brindar e dançar para celebrar o momento foi incentivada pelo irmão, que acompanhou os 11 anos da relação, marcados por desafios e escolhas. "Meu irmão Adolfo. Ele que sempre me apoiou e sempre soube de tudo que aconteceu", diz.

Ela espera que, com o vídeo, outras mulheres possam se sentir incentivadas a recomeçar uma nova história. "Que muitas mulheres entendam que encerrar um ciclo não é fracassar, é também ter coragem de escrever uma nova história", finalizou.

articles.title: Pedágio eletrônico começa a funcionar neste sábado (10) na MT-130 | G1
articles.standfirst: Modelo substitui as praças físicas de pedágio e permite que os veículos passem pelos pórticos sem precisar parar.
articles.summary: Modelo substitui as praças físicas de pedágio e permite que os veículos passem pelos pórticos sem precisar parar.
articles.body:
Pedágio no sistema de fluxo livre, também conhecido como "free flow" — Foto: Secom-MT

A cobrança de pedágio eletrônico na MT-130, no trecho entre Primavera do Leste e Paranatinga , começou neste sábado (10), com a implantação do sistema de fluxo livre, conhecido como free flow. O modelo substitui as praças físicas de pedágio e permite que os veículos passem pelos pórticos sem precisar parar.

Para veículos de passeio, a tarifa básica passa de R$ 2,55 para R$ 2,64 no pórtico PFF-01 e de R$ 3,85 para R$ 3,98 nos pórticos PFF-02 a PFF-06, a partir de quarta-feira (14), devido ao reajuste anual previsto no contrato de concessão.

🔍Pórtico PFF é uma estrutura metálica instalada sobre a rodovia para a cobrança de pedágio eletrônico. A sigla PFF significa Pórtico Free Flow, e os números identificam cada ponto de cobrança.

O reajuste foi aprovado por unanimidade pela Diretoria Executiva Colegiada da Agência Estadual de Regulação dos Serviços Públicos Delegados de Mato Grosso (Ager), durante a 16ª Sessão Regulatória, realizada na sexta-feira (9).

Os valores para as demais categorias de veículos seguem os critérios de classificação veicular e as regras previstas no Contrato de Concessão nº 008/2021.

No sistema free flow, não há cancelas nem necessidade de parar em praças físicas de pedágio . Os pórticos são equipados com sensores que identificam a placa dos veículos ou a etiqueta eletrônica (TAG), usada para o pagamento automático da tarifa.

O pagamento pode ser feito pelo site da concessionária responsável pela rodovia, via Pix ou cartões de crédito e débito, por meio de TAG ou nos totens de autoatendimento disponíveis no Serviço de Atendimento ao Usuário (SAU) da rodovia. O prazo para quitar a tarifa é de até 30 dias .

articles.title: Two 14-year-old UK conservationists are recruiting 20 children, aged 8 to 13, to raise harvest mice at home and help rebuild their declining population
articles.summary: Two 14-year-old conservationists in Devon, England, are inviting children to take part in an unusual wildlife project: raising tiny harvest mice at home
articles.body: Two 14-year-old conservationists in Devon, England, are inviting children to take part in an unusual wildlife project: raising tiny harvest mice at home before releasing them into the wild. Eva Wishart and Emily Smith, who bred mice in their garages and bedrooms before releasing 250 of them, are expanding their initiative, called Wild Pets, by recruiting 20 Devon-based children aged 8 to 13. Participants will receive a pair of mice and all necessary equipment after a training day next spring at Rewilding Coombeshead, and will breed the animals with guidance. The project aims to release 250 harvest mice into the wild by September 2027. Applications are made through wild-pets.org.How two teenagers came up with the unusual conservation planWild Pets began with Eva, who developed the idea after running her own harvest mouse breeding programme from the age of ten, and was later joined by her schoolfriend Emily. With two breeding pairs from the rewilding specialist Derek Gow, some borrowed tanks and no licence needed to breed or release native harvest mice, the pair raised mice in 27 tanks, using honeysuckle and hazel branches to create natural habitats. Last year they released 250 harvest mice into a nature reserve near Tiverton, using a soft-release enclosure built with a local carpenter’s help, with tiny holes that let the mice move freely while keeping out predators such as rats and snakes. The project was financed by around £4,000 raised through crowdfunding. Chris Packham attended a release in 2025 and, on Springwatch in June, called the idea “truly sensational.”Why children are being asked to raise harvest mice at homeThe project aims to increase the number of harvest mice that can be returned to suitable wild habitats. By involving children in the breeding process, Wishart and Smith also hope to make wildlife conservation more accessible to young people. Participants will be supported by experienced conservationists, with Gow advising. The Devon Environment Foundation gave the pair an earlier grant of £500. Organisers aim to breed and release 250 mice by September 2027, although success will depend on breeding outcomes and the animals’ ability to survive after release.Why harvest mice need conservation supportHarvest mice are Britain’s smallest rodents, known for weaving intricate nests among tall grasses and other vegetation. The Mammal Society classes them as Near Threatened across Great Britain, because changes to farming and land management have reduced their available habitat. The mice depend on vegetation that provides food, shelter and nesting sites, which makes them vulnerable when field margins are altered or removed. The earlier release has already shown encouraging signs: the following winter, Wishart and Smith found five maternity nests at the site, showing the mice had survived and begun reproducing.A project designed to inspire the next generationWild Pets is intended to do more than increase harvest mouse numbers. The teenagers hope that giving children direct experience of caring for wildlife will encourage a lasting interest in conservation and show how young people can help protect native species. The idea was a runner-up in Blue Peter’s Earthshot competition, and the project plans to extend the approach to other native species, including common lizards, stag beetles and glowworms. Its longer-term impact will depend on whether the breeding programme produces healthy animals that establish themselves in the wild, but the initiative offers an unusual example of youth-led conservation that combines practical participation with efforts to address biodiversity loss.You use AI every day. articles.title: Canada removed 7,300 cubic metres of toxic sediment from this harbour; fish species returned after disappearing for more than 30 years
articles.summary: Collingwood Harbour in Ontario, Canada, was once so degraded that it was named a Great Lakes area of concern in 1987.
articles.body: Collingwood Harbour in Ontario, Canada, was once so degraded that it was named a Great Lakes area of concern in 1987. Heavy metals contaminated its sediment, nuisance algae spread through its water, and fish habitat was lost. Restoration followed as 7,300 cubic metres of contaminated sediment were cleaned up, sewage treatment was improved, wetlands were protected, and new spawning beds and shoreline habitat were created. Fish species such as yellow pickerel and northern pike returned after an absence of more than thirty years. Read on to learn what was removed, what was rebuilt, who helped, and why it still matters today.Why Collingwood Harbour became a Great Lakes area of concern in 1987According to the Canada Water Agency, Collingwood Harbour was designated an area of concern in 1987 under the Canada-United States Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. A long history of industrialisation, urbanisation and agricultural land use along its shores and tributaries had degraded the harbour's environmental quality.Officials identified nine out of fourteen beneficial use impairments. These are measures of how poor water quality affects the environment, human health and the local economy. A tenth beneficial use was flagged as "requiring further assessment," meaning more information was needed to decide whether it was impaired.Cleanup of 7,300 cubic metres of sediment contaminated with heavy metalsOne of the most visible parts of the recovery was the removal of contaminated sediment from the harbour bed. The Canada Water Agency reports that 7,300 cubic metres of sediment holding heavy metals were cleaned up. The metals were copper, lead, zinc and chromium.Contaminated sediment is a long-term problem because the pollutants settle in the bottom of the water body, where they can harm bottom-dwelling organisms and work their way up the food chain.Cleaning up sediment was only part of the work. The Canada Water Agency explains that improvements to the Collingwood municipal sewage treatment plant reduced phosphorus loads by 63 per cent. Annual loads fell from 5,333 kilograms to 1,923 kilograms.Phosphorus feeds algae, so less of it meant fewer nuisance algae blooms in the harbour. That helped make conditions better for the fish and wildlife that depend on it.Wetland protection, fish spawning beds and stream habitat brought yellow pickerel and northern pike backRestoring the harbour also meant rebuilding the places where wildlife live and breed. The Canada Water Agency notes that local policies were changed to protect the 96-hectare Collingwood Wetland Complex. Crews also created more than five kilometres of stream and shoreline habitat, rehabilitated 20 hectares of wetlands, and added fish spawning beds, mostly along Black Ash Creek.The results showed up in the water. Prey fish increased, and species such as yellow pickerel and northern pike returned after an absence of more than thirty years.In 1994, Collingwood Harbour became the first Canadian area of concern to be officially delistedAn area of concern is delisted only when monitoring shows that the targets for every beneficial use impairment have been met and environmental quality has been restored. The Canada Water Agency states that Collingwood Harbour reached that point in 1994, making it the first Canadian area of concern to be delisted.All the beneficial uses are no longer considered impaired. They include restrictions on fish and wildlife consumption, degradation of fish and wildlife populations, bird or animal deformities or reproduction problems, degradation of bottom-dwelling organisms, restrictions on dredging activities, eutrophication or undesirable algae, beach closings, degradation of aesthetics, degradation of phytoplankton and zooplankton populations, and loss of fish and wildlife habitat.Local governments and conservation groups who made the restoration possibleThe Canada Water Agency emphasises that the work took scientific and technical expertise, local knowledge and hard work. It was carried out in partnership with other levels of government, non-government groups, Indigenous communities and members of the public.The partners it names include Canadian National Railway, the Collingwood Naturalist Club, the Environment Network of Collingwood, the Georgian Triangle Anglers Association, Nacan Products Limited, the Nottawasaga Valley Conservation Authority, the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry, the Ontario Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks, and the Town of Collingwood.You use AI every day. articles.title: A marble bust sat in an English garden for 70 years; it was actually a rare work by America’s first professional female sculptor
articles.summary: A routine house valuation in the Cotswolds has revealed that a weathered marble bust left in an English garden for more than 70 years was a rare work by
articles.body: A routine house valuation in the Cotswolds has revealed that a weathered marble bust left in an English garden for more than 70 years was a rare work by Harriet Goodhue Hosmer, widely regarded as America’s first professional female sculptor. The 1854 sculpture, depicting the Greek mythological figure Daphne, had been treated as an ordinary garden ornament and was covered with lichen. Its discovery has brought renewed attention to one of Hosmer’s earliest works, of which only a small number of marble versions are known to survive.The rare marble bust remained unrecognised for over 70 yearsThe sculpture was found during a routine house valuation in the Cotswolds by Thomas Jenner-Fust, director of Chorley’s Auctioneers. According to the BBC, the bust had spent more than seven decades outside and had become so familiar to the family that its real significance went unnoticed.The owners believed they had a reconstituted stone garden bust rather than an important 19th-century artwork. Covered in moss and lichen, it did little to suggest that it was carved from valuable marble. Jenner-Fust recognised that there was more to the object during his inspection and began examining it more closely.The discovery was particularly striking because the sculpture was not merely an old decorative piece. It was identified as a work by Harriet Goodhue Hosmer, an American artist whose career challenged the expectations placed on women in the 19th century. The BBC reports that Hosmer is widely regarded as the first professional female sculptor in the United States.What does the sculpture depictThe bust represents Daphne, a figure from Greek mythology who was pursued by Apollo. In the story, Daphne rejected the idea of marriage and sought protection from her father, who transformed her into a laurel tree. Hosmer captured the character at the point of this transformation.The Metropolitan Museum of Art provides important context for Hosmer’s treatment of Daphne through its own marble version of the subject. Its collection records that Hosmer carved Daphne in 1854, after designing the work in 1853. The Met version shows the bust ending in laurel branches, referring directly to Daphne’s transformation. The museum also notes that the subject had a personal resonance for Hosmer, who rejected traditional expectations surrounding women and relationships.The newly identified English bust carries another important clue to its origin. An inscription on the back includes Hosmer’s name and the Latin phrase me fecit Romae, meaning that she made it in Rome. The BBC reported that the inscription, together with the quality of the carving and the laurel leaves at the base, helped establish the sculpture as an authentic Hosmer work.Harriet Hosmer was important in her timeHosmer was born in Massachusetts in 1830 and built much of her professional life in Rome. During the 19th century, sculpture was overwhelmingly dominated by men, making her success particularly unique.The BBC describes Hosmer as a pioneering artist and feminist figure who developed an international reputation while working in a male-dominated profession. She was also openly gay at a time when same-sex relationships were widely condemned and, in some places, illegal.OnlyGoodNewsDaily describes Hosmer as a celebrated artist and feminist icon, noting that she spent a significant part of her early career in Italy among a circle of women sculptors. The publication also highlights how unusual it was for women to pursue professional artistic careers during the period.Her career therefore gives the garden discovery a significance beyond its financial value. The bust is evidence of the work of a woman who established herself internationally at a time when women faced considerable barriers to doing so.How rare is the garden sculptureThe scarcity of Hosmer’s Daphne makes the discovery especially notable. Historians at the Metropolitan Museum of Art recognise only 3 verified marble versions surviving today, with those examples held by museums in the United States.The Met itself has one of these versions. Its collection identifies the work as Daphne, made by Harriet Goodhue Hosmer, with the sculpture carved in marble and dated to 1853, carved 1854. The museum records its dimensions as about 69.9 centimetres high, 49.8 centimetres wide and 31.8 centimetres deep.That context helps explain why the identification of another version in an English garden was so unexpected. What had looked like an ageing outdoor ornament turned out to belong to a very small group of surviving works connected to Hosmer’s early career.What happened after the sculpture was identifiedOnce its importance became clear, the bust was acquired by Chorley’s Auctioneers in Gloucester. The BBC reported that it was expected to fetch as much as £18,000 when offered for sale.The sculpture was subsequently put up for auction in September, although later reporting stated that it did not sell. A further sale was planned, keeping the newly identified work in the spotlight.The history of the bust before its discovery remains uncertain. According to the BBC, the family believed an ancestor had bought it at auction during the mid-20th century. Black-and-white photographs from the 1950s also showed the sculpture already standing in the garden, providing evidence that it had been part of the property’s landscape for decades.The discovery brings a little-known chapter of American art history into view. Hosmer’s work survived decades of exposure in an English garden before its identity was recognised, while her other versions of Daphne now sit within museum collections.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 21-year-old Mexican environmental innovator is developing microbial fuel cells that use discarded materials to generate electricity and improve polluted water; her project aims to produce 50 working units by 2027
articles.summary: Growing up in Cuautlancingo, a town in Mexico’s Puebla state, Maritza Sanchez saw pollution close to home.
articles.body: Growing up in Cuautlancingo, a town in Mexico’s Puebla state, Maritza Sanchez saw pollution close to home. Now 21, she is developing microbial fuel cells that use materials recovered from local waste to generate electricity and help improve polluted water. Her project, Aquayac Energy, is focused on the Atoyac River, one of the waterways affected by serious contamination. The goal is ambitious but specific: refine her prototypes and produce 50 functional fuel cells by 2027. Earth Island Institute announced Sanchez as one of the 2026 Brower Youth Award winners, recognising her work alongside five other young environmental leaders. The award highlights not a finished technology, but a young innovator testing whether a small-scale, locally designed system can address two urgent needs at once: cleaner water and access to energy.A problem close to homeSanchez’s interest in pollution grew from what she observed around her. Earth Island Institute’s announcement says Cuautlancingo is surrounded by pollution, and that this experience helped shape her idea as a high school student. She began exploring whether discarded materials could be repurposed into a system that might both produce electricity and improve water quality.The project centres on the Atoyac River, which is heavily contaminated. Water pollution can affect communities in many ways, from the health of the river ecosystem to the quality of water people encounter in their daily lives. Sanchez’s idea is to test whether microbial fuel cells could offer a local tool for treating some wastewater while generating useful energy.Her project is called Aquayac Energy. The name reflects its connection to the Atoyac and the effort to turn an environmental challenge into a practical experiment. Rather than approaching pollution only as a problem to document, Sanchez is building and testing a technology that could make use of materials already available in the community, as per the report.How microbial fuel cells workMicrobial fuel cells use microorganisms to break down organic matter. As microbes consume that material, they release electrons, which can be captured by electrodes and used to generate a small electrical current. In Sanchez’s concept, the system uses discarded local materials and wastewater as part of the process. The technology is being researched in different settings, but Sanchez’s work is at the prototype stage. She designs and constructs the cells, tests their performance and measures how much energy they produce. She also examines water quality after treatment, assessing whether the process changes the condition of the water, it further shared.Those measurements matter because producing electricity alone would not make a system useful if it did not also treat water effectively. Similarly, a treatment process would need to be assessed for safety, consistency and suitability before anyone could rely on it. Sanchez’s work therefore involves testing more than one outcome, with the design still being refined.The technology is not a substitute for large-scale wastewater infrastructure or comprehensive river clean-up. Instead, it is an early-stage effort to see whether a compact, locally built system can contribute to solutions in places facing pollution and limited access to energy.Building and testing prototypesThrough Aquayac Energy, Sanchez has been designing, constructing and testing microbial fuel cell prototypes. The work includes checking the quality of water after treatment and measuring the amount of electricity the cells generate. These tests help her understand what is working, where the design needs improvement and whether the results can be repeated.The challenge is partly technical and partly practical. A successful prototype must function reliably, use materials that can be sourced and maintained, and produce results that can be measured. If the system is eventually used in communities, it would also need to be safe and suited to local conditions.That is why Sanchez’s 2027 target is framed around working units. She expects to scale the project over the coming year and produce 50 functional fuel cells. The goal provides a concrete measure of progress, moving beyond a concept towards a larger group of prototypes that can be evaluated.The award announcement does not claim that the cells are already supplying electricity to households or that they have solved pollution in the Atoyac. Instead, it describes an ongoing effort to refine the design and test its environmental and energy outcomes.Recognition and a next phaseEarth Island Institute selected Sanchez as one of six 2026 Brower Youth Award recipients. The annual award recognises young leaders whose work is contributing to environmental change in North America and beyond. The institute said the projects recognised this year ranged from habitat restoration and pollinator protection to school climate action and technologies for wastewater.The award also offers more than public recognition. Earth Island Institute says recipients receive leadership training, networking opportunities and a platform to amplify their work. For a project still developing its prototypes, those connections may help Sanchez share results, find collaborators and build support for the next stage.Sanchez’s work stands out because it brings together environmental concerns that are often handled separately. Waste, water quality and energy access each demand their own solutions, but her project asks whether one process might help with more than one of them. Whether microbial fuel cells can make a lasting contribution will depend on what further testing shows.A local idea with a measurable goalThe most immediate milestone is the planned production of 50 functional fuel cells by 2027. Reaching that target would allow Sanchez to work with more units, gather additional data and better understand how the technology performs. It would not, by itself, establish that the system is ready for widespread use, but it could take the project from early experimentation to a more substantial stage of evaluation.Sanchez’s approach begins with the conditions around her. She is responding to pollution in her community by designing a technology that draws on local discarded materials and targets wastewater. The work combines invention with careful measurement, checking both energy generation and water quality rather than relying on promises.For now, Aquayac Energy remains a project in development. Its significance lies in the questions it is testing and the commitment to build, measure and refine the technology. At 21, Sanchez is turning a concern rooted in her home region into an engineering challenge with a clear next step: 50 working units, and better evidence about what they can do.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Are students Chambal dacoits?’: Abhijeet Dipke’s parents slam Delhi Police crackdown
articles.summary: CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: Parents of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) convenor Abhijeet Dipke on Saturday criticised the detention of their son and hundreds
articles.body: CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: Parents of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) convenor Abhijeet Dipke on Saturday criticised the detention of their son and hundreds of protesters in Delhi ahead of the party’s proposed demonstration against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, questioning the heavy police deployment and accusing the government of undermining democracy.Dipke’s father asked whether students protesting over electoral issues were “Chambal dacoits”, while his mother questioned why the protesters had been detained from a flight.Delhi Police launched a sweeping crackdown in the national capital, detaining Dipke, YouTuber Dhruv Rathee and nearly 500 protesters, foiling their attempt to reach Jantar Mantar for the planned CJP demonstration.Dipke’s father questions police deploymentAbhijeet’s father, Bhagwan Dipke, questioned the deployment of a large police force for what he described as a student agitation.''I don't understand why so much police force is deployed in Delhi? It is an agitation of students. Have dacoits from Chambal gathered in Delhi? Dacoits are sitting in Parliament," Bhagwan Dipke told reporters.When asked about the protest taking place without permission, he questioned the need for official clearance to demonstrate against the government."Why is permission needed when every Indian has a legal right to protest. This means they (government) don't follow democracy. How would they grant permission (to agitate) against them (government) when this protest is meant to expose them? There is no question of permission here.""He is Chandra Shekhar Azad and Bhagat Singh for me,'' he added.‘Do they arrest rapists like this?’: Abhijeet Dipke’s motherAbhijeet’s mother, Anita Dipke, also criticised the police action, questioning why protesters had been detained from an aircraft.''This is wrong on the part of the government. What have these people done that they had to be detained from a flight? Do they go to the houses of rapists and arrest them? They don't. But they arrested these people, including Abhijeet Dipke, when there was no need to do so," she added.Delhi Police detain over 1500 protestors ahead of CJP protestDelhi Police on Saturday detained around 1500 protesters while preventing them from gathering at Jantar Mantar for the proposed CJP demonstration against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Protesters were detained from several locations across the New Delhi area. Police were also using drones to monitor the movement of people attempting to reach the protest site.(With PTI inputs)Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. articles.title: 'What are you so scared of?': TMC calls Mamata Banerjee's detention 'Super Emergency', targets PM Narendra Modi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The All India Trinamool Congress (TMC) on Saturday launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the central government after
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The All India Trinamool Congress (TMC) on Saturday launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the central government after former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee and several party MPs were allegedly detained by Delhi Police during a protest in the national capital.Calling the police action a sign of a "Super Emergency" and a "dark day for democracy", the party accused the authorities of curbing the constitutional right to dissent. It alleged that the leaders were barred from raising slogans or displaying posters before being forced into police vans and taken to an undisclosed location.In a post on X, the party's official handle said, "Super emergency is going on - @MamataOfficial While our Hon’ble Chairperson along with our Hon’ble MPs were peacefully protesting, Delhi Police came and instructed that no slogans and no posters were allowed. Why? "The party further alleged, "Then, they unlawfully forced our Chairperson and our MPs into a police van and are now taking them to an undisclosed location. Why? @narendramodi what are you so scared of? Have you simply forgotten that India is a democratic country and every single person has the right to protest?"Criticising Delhi Police and the Union government, the TMC said, "@DelhiPolice how dare you? Since when did arresting peaceful protesters become the norm in our democracy? When peaceful dissent is met with arrests instead of dialogue, it raises serious questions about the state of our democratic values," the party wrote.Issuing a stern message to the ruling dispensation, the party said, "The Mo–Shah duo may continue to push the limits, but no government is above accountability, and no power is permanent. @narendramodi, REMEMBER THAT! A dark day for democracy. A reminder that the fight to protect it must never stop…"TMC Rajya Sabha MP Samirul Islam also criticised the authorities, alleging that detained party leaders were being driven around Delhi in a police vehicle without being informed of their destination.In a post on X, Samirul Islam wrote, "Is this a Super Emergency? For the past one and a half hours, we have been driving around the entire city of Delhi, and we don't know what they are going to do with us. Isn't this a Super Emergency?"The remarks came shortly after Delhi Police detained a delegation of TMC parliamentarians and leaders protesting in central Delhi. Visuals from the site showed security personnel escorting the leaders into police vans.Meanwhile, around 1,000 protesters had been detained across the national capital by Saturday while attempting to march towards Jantar Mantar for a Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Delhi Police sources said.Police continued to take demonstrators into preventive custody after informing them that permission had not been granted for the gathering.CJP activist Abhijeet Dipke, who travelled from Mumbai to Delhi to participate in the protest, posted a video on Instagram alleging that police personnel detained him and his associates as they disembarked from their flight at Delhi airport.In the video, Dipke alleged that police personnel entered the aircraft and attempted to detain them."So, you can see that Delhi Police is entering the plane to arrest us. They are all entering the plane. We just landed. All the Delhi Police officers are standing in the aisle. They are trying to arrest us from inside the plane. The entire Delhi Police is getting on the plane... This is the fear of Narendra Modi... Not even Indira Gandhi did this during the Emergency. All we wanted to do is a peaceful protest, and they are picking us up from the flight like we are criminals," he said.He further alleged, "You can see where the nation is heading. They are here to arrest us directly from the flight. This is something not even Indira Gandhi had done. This is dictatorship, where Delhi Police has entered the flight and is trying to arrest us. Come on, arrest us. We are here to be arrested. Come on, arrest us. We are here to be arrested... We are not afraid of you."Security personnel remained deployed at several locations across the national capital as CJP activists continued their call for a protest against the Election Commission of India (ECI). Entry points to Delhi were placed under heightened security, while 46 Metro stations remained closed, according to the details provided.As part of the security arrangements, the New Delhi district was divided into 20 operational zones, with dedicated detention centres established for each zone, police said."The New Delhi district has been divided into 20 zones, and dedicated detention centres have been set up for each zone. Stadiums across the national capital have also been converted into temporary detention centres," the police added. articles.title: Russian strikes kill 12 in Ukraine after Trump announces diesel deal with Putin
articles.summary: Russian attacks killed at least 12 people, including three children, in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on
articles.body: Russian attacks killed at least 12 people, including three children, in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday. The strikes came a day after US President Donald Trump announced an agreement to purchase Russian diesel, a move Kyiv warned could help fund Moscow’s war against Ukraine.Russian aerial bombs struck residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, leaving at least 14 people wounded, Zelenskyy said.Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange long-range aerial attacks, while their forces remain largely deadlocked along the front line, more than four and a half years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter an intensifying Russian bombardment campaign that has claimed more than 60 lives over the past four days.Trump announced on Friday that he had reached a deal to buy diesel from Russia, marking a significant departure from years of US pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. The move also comes as his administration seeks to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy wrote on X on Saturday.He said the attacks showed that Moscow interpreted any easing of pressure as an opportunity to continue its military campaign and strike Ukrainian cities. “Different signals are needed,” he added.Trump had been expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia with Russian President Vladimir Putin during a phone call. However, the US president announced the diesel deal on Friday instead.Under the agreement, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”, Trump said in an online post. Russia would then deliver another 3 million tonnes “within a short period of time”.The announcement appeared to contradict a sweeping Russia sanctions law Trump signed last month, which aimed to curb the oil and gas revenues that help finance Moscow’s war against Ukraine.Reacting to the agreement in a lengthy online post on Friday, Zelenskyy warned that Russia would repay the move with “further terror and perfidy”. He argued that the deal amounted to an investment in the war that could prolong the conflict.“It plays into Russia’s hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.According to a statement issued by the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, Zelenskyy described the agreement as “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners”.Trump announced the deal while his envoy, Steve witkoff, and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, were meeting Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war, according to AP.Zelenskyy questioned the circumstances surrounding the negotiations, suggesting that Ukraine’s delegation was being used to divert attention from the diesel agreement.“I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Kamala Harris faces pushback over 2028 presidential bid as husband, Democratic donors express doubts: Report
articles.summary: Former US vice president Kamala Harris is facing doubts over a possible 2028 presidential bid, with her husband, Doug Emhoff, privately expressing a
articles.body: Former US vice president Kamala Harris is facing doubts over a possible 2028 presidential bid, with her husband, Doug Emhoff, privately expressing a preference for her not to run again and some Democratic donors warning that another campaign would be a long shot.Emhoff has told people privately that he would prefer Harris to stay out of the presidential race, The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday. However, people close to the former second gentleman expect him to support his wife if she ultimately decides to seek the White House again, the report said.Some Democratic donors have also directly cautioned Harris about the prospects of another presidential campaign, amid concerns about her political future following her defeat to President Donald Trump in the 2024 election, the New York Post reported.Harris lost the Electoral College and every swing state to Trump in 2024, despite raising around $1.5 billion for her campaign. However, she continues to lead the hypothetical Democratic presidential field by double digits in several recent polls, keeping her in contention for the party's 2028 nomination.The former vice president has not announced whether she intends to run again, but her recent political activities have fuelled speculation about a possible return to the White House.Ahead of the November midterm elections, Harris has attended Democratic fundraisers, including private events supporting Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate David Crowley and Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, according to the Wall Street Journal.She also recently joined a call with the Democratic National Committee and more than 2,000 volunteers, urging them to support get-out-the-vote efforts across a dozen states.Speaking at a National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) event in Michigan in September, Harris said she had yet to decide whether to launch another presidential campaign."I have not decided if I’m going to run again," she said, adding that the immediate priority was the midterm elections. "I do sincerely believe ’28 won’t matter if we don’t get through ’26."Harris faces questions over political futureSome people who have known and worked with Harris remain sceptical that she will ultimately enter the 2028 presidential race, according to the Wall Street Journal.Harris became the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024 after then-president Joe Biden withdrew from the race, leaving her with just 107 days before the election. She went on to lose to Trump, who secured a second term in the White House.The defeat has left questions about Harris's standing within the Democratic Party and whether she can build a stronger campaign for another presidential run. Despite the setback, her continued engagement with Democratic candidates, donors and party activists suggests she intends to remain politically active.Harris had earlier ruled out running for California governor in 2026, leaving open the possibility of pursuing national office again. She has also indicated that her political career is not over.Meanwhile, Emhoff has taken up a position as a partner at Los Angeles law firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP. Harris and Emhoff also purchased an $8 million mansion in Malibu earlier this year.While her husband's reported reservations and concerns among some donors could complicate a potential campaign, Harris has not ruled out another presidential bid. For now, she has maintained that Democrats must focus on the 2026 midterm elections before turning their attention to the next presidential race.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ‘Haven’t you consumed pesticide yet?’: Telangana tahsildar’s remarks to farmer spark row
articles.summary: HYDERABAD: “Haven’t you consumed pesticide yet?
articles.body: HYDERABAD: “Haven’t you consumed pesticide yet? Are you still alive?” These are the remarks that Gajwel tahsildar P H Swamy allegedly made to a farmer who approached his office over a land dispute, triggering widespread criticism after a video of the exchange surfaced on social media.The video shows the farmer, Yesu, from Maktha Masanpally village in Gajwel mandal of Siddipet district, expressing distress over his situation and questioning the official’s response. When the farmer allegedly asked whether the tahsildar found his plight amusing, Swamy reportedly replied, “Yes, I do. Of course, I do.” The remarks have drawn criticism from social media users, with demands for senior revenue officials to look into the incident and take appropriate action.The farmer’s grievance was linked to compensation for agricultural land being acquired for the Regional Ring Road (RRR). The incident has raised questions over the manner in which a revenue official allegedly responded to a farmer seeking a resolution to a land-related problem.Speaking to TOI, Swamy said the video was old and offered his version of the events leading up to the exchange. He said Yesu had been visiting his office frequently and demanding the release of compensation for the land, which could not be acquired because of a dispute among family members over its partition.According to Swamy, he had repeatedly explained to the farmer that the acquisition and payment of compensation could proceed only after the family resolved the dispute. The tahsildar said Yesu had also threatened several times to consume pesticide if the money was not credited.Swamy said that on one occasion, the farmer arrived at his office in an intoxicated state and created a disturbance. He lodged a complaint with the police, who kept Yesu at the station for a day, warned him and sent him away. No FIR was registered in the matter, he said.Explaining the circumstances in which he made the remarks, Swamy said around 15 people were present in his room at the time and that the farmer had repeatedly threatened to consume pesticide. He added that the family subsequently resolved its land dispute, following which the land was acquired and compensation was credited to the family members’ accounts.However, the video has continued to draw criticism over the reported remarks and the way the farmer was addressed while seeking help with a land-related issue.Siddipet district revenue officer D Nagarajamma told TOI that she was not aware of the incident.As of Saturday, no inquiry had been ordered into the matter.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news. articles.title: ‘Rigged when you lose?’ 124 former bureaucrats defend EC & SIR, challenge vote-rigging claims
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A group of 124 former IAS, IFS and allied services officers has issued an open letter to citizens defending the Election Commission (EC) and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A group of 124 former IAS, IFS and allied services officers has issued an open letter to citizens defending the Election Commission (EC) and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, arguing that allegations of vote rigging must be backed by credible evidence.Citing safeguards in the electoral process, past election results and data from Bihar’s 2025 Assembly polls, the signatories have challenged claims questioning the credibility of the EC and the need for SIR.The officers said India's electoral system had evolved significantly from an era marked by booth capturing, ballot-box stuffing and electoral violence. They cited multiple safeguards in the present system, including polling agents, electronic voting machine (EVM) sealing, strong-room security and voter-verified paper audit trail (VVPAT) verification.Referring to the 2025 Bihar Assembly elections, the signatories said the polls recorded no re-polling and the highest voter turnout since 1951."A system cannot be honest when you win and rigged when you lose," the letter said, pointing out that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which leads the government at the Centre, had lost several state elections under the same EC and also lost its parliamentary majority in 2024.The signatories include former foreign secretary Kanwal Sibal and former IAS officers R D Kapur, Samirendra Chatterjee, Gopal Krishna, Vivek Bhardwaj and Navneet Sehgal.Defending the EC's independence, the officers highlighted its multi-member structure and institutional safeguards. They also drew a distinction between questioning the electoral process and substantiating allegations against it."Questioning is every citizen's right. Proving is the accuser's duty," the letter said.On SIR, the officers argued that the exercise was necessary to maintain accurate electoral rolls. Citing figures from Bihar, they referred to around 22 lakh deceased voters and seven lakh duplicate entries identified during the revision, alongside the addition of approximately 21.5 lakh new voters."An uncleaned roll does not protect the voter. It protects the fraudster," the letter said.The officers also pointed to safeguards available during SIR, including notices, hearings, appeals and the participation of political parties' booth-level agents. They said the Supreme Court had scrutinised the exercise, prescribed additional safeguards and upheld the EC's authority to undertake it.Concluding their argument, the signatories urged critics to examine allegations against the electoral system consistently, irrespective of election outcomes."If the system you call rigged is the same one that handed you your victories, ask yourself whether it is the system you doubt, or only the result," the letter said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: HC dismisses challenge to state textbook paper tender eligibility
articles.summary: Orissa HC dismissed a paper supplier’s plea against Odisha’s textbook paper tender, upholding eligibility terms and cautioning courts to intervene only for arbitrariness.
articles.body: Cuttack: Orissa high court has dismissed a private paper supplier’s challenge to state govt’s tender for procuring paper for textbooks, observing that tendering authorities have the freedom to frame eligibility conditions according to their requirements.A division bench of Chief Justice Harish Tandon and Justice Chittaranjan Dash, in its Oct 7 judgment, said courts should be cautious while examining administrative decisions on tender conditions and should not interfere unless arbitrariness or mala fide is established.“Every administrative action does not call for interference and, therefore, the court must put a great caution in interfering therewith,” the bench observed, dismissing the writ petition.The dispute concerned eligibility criteria in a tender floated by the directorate of textbook production and marketing on Sept 11 for procuring 26,450 metric tonnes of 70 GSM maplitho reel paper with watermark, measuring 84 cm. The technical bids were scheduled to open on Oct 8.Under the eligibility criteria, bidders were required to demonstrate experience in supplying maplitho virgin paper with watermark in quantities equivalent to at least 60% of the tendered quantity or a minimum of 11,000 metric tonnes annually during each of the preceding three consecutive years to govt or semi-govt departments and organisations.Rejecting the challenge, the bench found no arbitrariness in requiring bidders to have supplied the specified paper in the preceding years. It also took note of the authorities’ decision to consider objections and revise the quantity requirement after deliberations.“The court must respect the freedom into the tender inviting authorities for incorporating any terms and conditions which is reasonable, rational and does not inculcate any sense of arbitrariness or mala fide,” the judges said.The court further clarified that tendering authorities could tailor conditions to their specific needs and that the absence of a similar requirement in other states did not, by itself, make the condition liable to judicial interference.The petitioner had alleged that the condition was excessive, arbitrary and tailored to favour select suppliers. It argued that the watermark requirement had no direct connection with textbook printing and would unnecessarily exclude potential bidders. The experience criterion, it said, restricted competition by limiting participation to a handful of suppliers despite the availability of other capable firms.The objections were also raised by several prospective bidders during a pre-bid meeting. Following deliberations, the authorities issued a corrigendum on September 30, reducing the minimum annual supply requirement from 11,000 tonnes to 10,000 tonnes.Finding no grounds to interfere with the tender conditions or the corrigendum, high court dismissed the petition.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhubaneswar | Silver Rate in Bhubaneswar | Bank Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Public Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Petrol Price in Bhubaneswar | Diesel Price in Bhubaneswar | CNG Price in Bhubaneswar | LPG Price in BhubaneswarStay updated with the latest Bhubaneswar news. articles.title: Stones hurled at bus carrying detained protesters in Delhi’s Jhandewalan, cops injured
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Stones were pelted at a bus carrying detained protesters in Delhi’s Jhandewalan area on Saturday as police continued detaining people
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Stones were pelted at a bus carrying detained protesters in Delhi’s Jhandewalan area on Saturday as police continued detaining people attempting to reach Jantar Mantar for the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.Stone-pelting was also reported in other parts of the national capital, including Connaught Place and Imtiaz Ali Marg, where police personnel were injured, officials said.According to news agency IANS, the Jhandewalan incident occurred when police personnel were transporting detained individuals in a bus through the area. Officials said some protesters allegedly attempted to escape custody and damage the vehicle. Police subsequently detained them again and moved them to a designated location.Security was strengthened around Jhandewalan Metro Station, with heavy police deployment and traffic restrictions in place. The operation also led to traffic diversions in and around the area.In a separate incident near Imtiaz Ali Marg, close to Akashwani Bhawan, around 25 to 30 protesters allegedly jumped barricades and pelted security personnel with stones after attempting to reach the protest site, officials said. Two police personnel were injured in the incident, they added.Stone-pelting was also reported near Baba Kharak Singh Marg in Connaught Place as police attempted to disperse protesters and take them into preventive custody.Recounting the confrontation, Head Constable Nagendra told ANI, “We were removing the protesters. During that process, we faced a scuffle, and my nameplate got broken... It happened near the Arya School lane, close to Baba Kharak Singh Marg. There were several protesters. They were detained... There was stone-pelting; a stone even hit my shoe.”Police Inspector Vivek Kumar said a group advanced towards a small police contingent before reinforcements arrived.“It must have been about two hours ago. Seeing that we were few in number, they started advancing towards us. Some of them threw stones,” he said.“Fortunately, we escaped; just as they were closing in on us, our staff arrived from behind. We were saved... There must have been 60–70 people. No one was injured... No, none [protesters] were caught,” Kumar added.Police detained more than 1,000 protesters across Delhi, with some reports putting the figure at over 1,500, as authorities enforced restrictions and prevented demonstrators from reaching Jantar Mantar. articles.title: CJP at Jantar Mantar: 'Cockroach' group says leaders detained at Delhi protest
articles.summary: The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - want electoral reforms ahead of crucial state elections.
articles.body:
Hundreds of protesters have been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) calling for electoral reforms.

The group said its founder Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - was detained with other leaders shortly after landing in Delhi.

Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration, though the CJP insisted it would go ahead.

Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions, but had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital.

The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - are seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.

It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.

Under Kumar's leadership, India's election commission has undertaken a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - it said this was a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.

But in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.

The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.

The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.

Before arriving in Delhi, the CJP's founder Dipke said: "If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail or trying to intimidate us with the fear of imprisonment, you are mistaken."

He and and two other leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained on their flight from Mumbai on Saturday.

The group claimed the three men have been taken to an undisclosed location. Delhi Police have not commented.

Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's new designated leader while the others are in detention, released a video telling protesters that "if Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar".

Student activist Neha Bora, who had also been detained by Delhi Police, urged demonstrators to "hold the line".

The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks.

Announcements could be heard across the city, asking people to co-operate with the police.

One protester, Sabika Muzaffar, told the BBC she and her mother expected to be detained.

"On the way to the protest site, instead of reciting hymns and verses as we usually do, my mother and I were rote learning our lawyer's number," she said.

She said that showing up to protest was "her way of defending the country and its democracy".

A few minutes after Muzaffar spoke to the BBC she was taken away by police.

Several trains to and from major Delhi stations had been cancelled and dozens of metro stations were closed from Friday night.

Buses packed with detained protesters were seen being driven away from the protest site.

The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted.

Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"

The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.

In July, Dipke watched from the stage as the five-week-long protest ended in celebration after the resignation of India's education minister.

articles.title: India’s ‘Cockroach’ leaders detained; New Delhi in lockdown
articles.summary: Indian police crackdown appears to have prevented mass protests against the country’s election chief from taking place.
articles.body:
Police in India’s capital New Delhi have detained more than 1,000 protesters, opposition politicians, journalists, student union leaders, lawyers and the founders of the “Cockroach” youth movement in an effort to quash their demonstration demanding the resignation of the election chief.

The satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other youth groups had announced a protest in the subcontinent’s capital for Saturday, aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR).

The protesters accuse the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of using the SIR to sway election results, ‌in collusion with its appointees in the election commission, including Kumar.

Meanwhile, opposition parties say the voter deletions also affected the outcome of some recent state elections won by the BJP, and have cast a shadow on elections in the world’s largest democracy.

The CJP had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in central Delhi.

But on Saturday, the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.

The Indian capital was also in lockdown with thousands of police and paramilitary personnel deployed across the city, trains to New Delhi cancelled, mobile internet services suspended and metro stations and markets shuttered, in an effort to stop the protests.

BJP spokesman Sambit Patra has dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchic elements”.

“Their flop show has been completely demolished,” Patra said. “What is happening at Jantar Mantar, what you can see on TV and a few social media handles, is not India’s story. India is calm and going ahead under good governance,” he told reporters.

Police detained the founder of ⁠the CJP Abhijeet Dipke, as well as his associates Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, in an aeroplane upon arrival at New Delhi from Mumbai.

Dipke shared a video on his Instagram channel, showing a team of police officers entering the Air India plane after it landed. As they came closer, he said: “I have come to get arrested. I am not afraid of you guys.”

In another video shared by Ranka, Dipke was seen addressing the other passengers on the flight.

“It was nice to know you all. We can see where the nation is heading,” he said. “This is dictatorship where Delhi police has entered in the flight and trying to arrest us.”

Delhi police also detained other CJP members, YouTuber and Modi critic Dhruv Rathee , Neha Bora, the national president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), a leftist group affiliated with the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist), Dipankar Bhattacharya, the general secretary of the party, Prashant Bhushan, a senior lawyer at the Supreme Court, politicians Yogendra Yadav and Mamata Banerjee, among others.

Despite the detentions of the founders of the youth movement, small protests took place elsewhere in the city, including at the popular crafts market “Dilli Haat”.

But journalists trying to cover these protests and people attempting to protest anywhere in the capital were also detained and whisked away in police buses.

Shranaya, a state committee member of the left-wing Students’ Federation of India (SFI), who goes by her first name, told Al Jazeera that their office in New Delhi had been under surveillance for hours, but members inside had managed to escape and protest.

“This is dictatorship live and in front of us, just to protect a bureaucrat who steals elections for the BJP on Modi’s behest. They are murdering democracy in the daylight in the Indian capital,” she said.

“This government is unaware of the power of the people, and that is our upper hand. We do not have weapons, but we have zeal. We will be again on the streets, and we will keep returning,” she added. “We are students. We are unemployed. We are ‘cockroaches’ – and we will return.”

She then climbed a barricade but was dragged away by police and taken away in a bus.

The opposition Congress party’s president, Mallikarjun Kharge slammed Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government after the detentions.

“Modi government has turned the ‘Mother of Democracy’ into a ‘Muzzled Democracy’!” he posted on X. “Detentions, arrests, jails, lathis [batons] and pellets cannot deter the people of India. Since the days of our freedom struggle, the youth have been at the forefront of shaping the nation’s destiny,” he added.

Global human rights group Amnesty International warned that the detentions signal the Indian government’s desperate attempts to “supress critical voices”.

“The authorities must immediately and unconditionally release all those who have been detained solely for exercising their right to Freedom of Expression and Right to peaceful assembly,” Aakar Patel, chair of board of Amnesty International India, told Al Jazeera.

The Committee to Protect Journalists urged Indian police to “respect journalists”.

“We call on the Delhi Police to immediately release all detained journalists and media workers and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests in Delhi and the police response without interference,” Kunal Majumder, CPJ’s Asia Pacific programme coordinator, told Al Jazeera.

The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls in advance of recent state polls.

The unrest is also coming before a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027.

Sanjay Kapoor, editor of Hard News Magazine and a political analyst, told Al Jazeera that it is “very strange” to see Modi’s government “so panic-driven and fearful of what the protesters might do”.

“The truth is that the BJP and the centre have been very, very scared of how it will all play out,” he said.

Kapoor noted that most of the people coming to the protests do not want Modi’s BJP to continue to govern.

“Modi’s government has begun to lose a lot of credibility at the moment,” he said. “BJP is afraid that the ground has shifted dramatically against them and they would find it very difficult to come back to power,” he added.
