articles.title: ‘Anachronism’: Rubio’s civilisational rhetoric prompts pushback from Iran
articles.summary: Rubio says threats to Western civilisation today ‘every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity’.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – A speech by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio invoking memories of ancient Persia has been met with coldness or disdain across the Iranian political spectrum amid Washington’s ongoing war on Iran.

With the Acropolis in Athens as a backdrop, Rubio presented the United States, founded in the 18th century, as the inheritor of ancient Western civilisation running from Greece to Rome.

During the speech, he argued that modern-day Western countries have lost their confidence, weakened their industries and militaries, and need renewed ambition and power in the future.

Referencing the ancient Greco-Persian Wars, he used the Persian destruction of Athens in 480 BC under King Xerxes I as an example of Western civilisation surviving an external enemy.

“The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines and razed the Acropolis to the ground,” Rubio said. He subsequently hailed the return of the Athenians and the construction of the Parthenon under Pericles.

The top US diplomat also directed his rhetoric against Iran’s current leaders, who have been in power since a 1979 Islamic revolution, calling them “fanatics” who run a “death cult” that wields martyrdom as a tool to achieve their political objectives.

“The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity,” Rubio claimed. He boasted that the choice of President Donald Trump’s administration was the “unapologetic pursuit of national power”.

The US and Iran have been at war since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28. While fighting between the two sides has subsided, the US has continued a naval blockade on Iran while shipping through the vital Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted.

Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, and parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf both responded by invoking the Roman Emperor Valerian, who was captured alive by Persian King Shapur I’s forces in battle in 260 AD.

“Anyone who brings history into this must be prepared for its repetition,” Rezaei said.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused Rubio of flattening Greek, Roman, Christian and modern history.

It also accused the secretary of state of incorporating an “America First” narrative to legitimise a military escalation against Iran after a relative decrease in fighting since June when a now-defunct memorandum of understanding was agreed .

“It appears that the US has concluded it is better to justify its policy of coercion and force to the world under the beautiful neon lights of ‘philosophy of history’, instead of naked bullying that uses the language of cowboys,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said in a statement. He added that Rubio was resorting to “anachronism”, rehashing long buried historical events for modern-day legitimacy.

After the 2020 assassination of Qassem Soleimani, a commander in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Trump threatened to hit 52 Iranian sites “very hard”, including places “important to Iran & the Iranian culture”.

Since February, the US has been criticised for damaging Iranian historical and cultural sites during its bombing of Iran.

Culture Minister Reza Salehi-Amiri urged Western politicians to speak about Iran with a “language of respect” since “it is not an enemy created in a political speech but a living civilisation, a great nation and a lasting reality in world history” that dates back millennia.

Iranian historian Touraj Daryaei told local media on Friday that while Rubio’s account of the sack of Athens was true, he omitted an important fact cited by Greek historian Herodotus and others – a major motivation for the Persian attack was retaliation.

In 498 BC, Athens’ forces burned Sardis, a provincial Persian capital in western Anatolia. For Iranians who feel they were subject to an unprovoked attack by the US and Israel, this event could have modern-day relevance.

Shima, a 26-year-old resident of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that she did not appreciate Rubio’s attempt to use conflicts 2,500 years ago to muster support for the ongoing war with Iran.

“They want to continue the war, and they will say whatever they think will work in the moment,” she said.

During his January 2025 Senate confirmation hearing, Rubio had referred to Iranians as “the people of an ancient civilisation and culture with tremendous pride and advances who take great pride in their Persian heritage and identity”.

“I don’t know of any nation on Earth in which there’s a bigger difference between the people and those who govern them,” he said at the time. “In no way are the clerics who run the country representative of the people and its history and contributions it’s made to humanity.”

But the US war on Iran, its naval blockade of southern Iranian ports and isolating sanctions have not had the worst impact on Iran’s government and leaders but on Iranians themselves and have failed to change the behaviour of the government.

Trump’s comments on the potential “death of a civilisation” in Iran in case of a military escalation have instilled more pessimism among Iranians about the goals of the US war, which was initially cited as an attempt to free the people from their government.

Most Iranians reacted negatively to Rubio’s latest speech although some members of the diaspora or others opposed to the Islamic Republic argued that the US secretary of state is against Iranian authorities, not an entire ancient civilisation.

Iranian state media were quick to slam Rubio for his remarks with the hardline Vatan-e Emrouz newspaper on Saturday publishing a front page image of Rubio in ancient Roman military attire and holding a shield and sword.

“Ancient war” read the headline. The newspaper claimed that Rubio was trying to “create historical-ideological backing for the US war against Iran”.

Vali Nasr, professor of international affairs and Middle East studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, DC, told Al Jazeera he believes Rubio’s aim was to define a common enemy for the US and Europe to rebuild their relations around.

“He decided that Iran, rather than Islam, which was previously viewed as the civilisational enemy, should play that role to bind the West together,” he said. “It also reflects US frustration that Europe has not played a major role in the war and seeks to paper over deep divisions between the US and Europe on Russia and Ukraine.”

Rubio delivered his speech as Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to sell diesel fuel to the US and global markets despite sanctions on Russia. The US president said the agreement would lower diesel prices, which have risen to record levels due to the Iran war. Nasr said Trump’s announcement and Rubio’s speech together could be a message by the administration that Iran and not Russia is the enemy the West should be focused on.

“I think whether this rhetoric would alienate Iranians was no more a concern than President [George W] Bush’s Islamophobia was a concern alienating Muslims,” Nasr told Al Jazeera. “However, it makes clear that Washington sees no difference between Iranians and Iran as a civilisation and the Islamic Republic.”

articles.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft
articles.summary: War-driven prices for silver are threatening nagra makers in northern India.
articles.body:
In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not. Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted.

The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts.

For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras.

He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal. Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place.

Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair. Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s.

Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh.

“Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842.

“They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added.

Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike.

“Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained. “The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.”

Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand.

“In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said. “But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.”

There are two types of silver nagras — open-toed chappals and closed-toed jutis, and customers can choose different patterns, ornamentation and designs.

articles.title: Hundreds protest in Caernarfon over data centre plans
articles.summary: Placard-waving opponents highlight concerns about a data centre development on the local landscape.
articles.body:
Hundreds of people have taken part in a protest against plans to build a new data centre because of concerns about its effects on the area.

Developers want to construct a complex on a 101 acre site between Caernarfon and Y Felinheli, in Gwynedd, saying it could create more than 900 jobs during construction and 200 permanent roles.

About 300 gathered for a rally in Caernarfon to highlight their opposition. More than 22,500 have signed a petition opposing the plan .

Canolfan Ddata Menai has previously said its proposals would "transform and revitalise the long-derelict" site as well as offer significant employment.

But opponent Ernest Dyson, who lives near the proposed site, said it was "basically the destruction of the most beautiful part of the Menai Strait".

"It is quite incredible it should come to this.

"The people of the area are custodians of it. That's what we must think of," he said.

Liz Saville Roberts, the Plaid Cymru MP for Dwyfor Meirionnydd, said: "We know that we need data centres but they have to be the right size, the right technology and in the right places.

"We need proper regulations and we need to make sure that communities benefit from this.

"We have too long a history in Wales of extractive industries that left nothing behind and have little benefit for communities.

"That mustn't happen again in the 21st Century."

Canolfan Ddata Menai said the project would ensure "continued use" of the surrounding area , including Lôn Las Menai cycleway and footpath, and would have "no undue impact" on the Menai Strait and an associated site of special scientific interest (SSSI).

articles.title: New rulebook for rogue pilots? Flydubai attack puts 9/11-era aviation security in doubt
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The attack by a Flydubai co-pilot on the captain during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has renewed questions about whether aviation security
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The attack by a Flydubai co-pilot on the captain during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has renewed questions about whether aviation security needs another overhaul, 25 years after the September 11 attacks transformed how airlines protect their aircraft.The September 30 incident saw the aircraft plunge around 16,000 feet in 30 seconds after the co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain with an emergency crash axe. The aircraft was eventually brought under control and landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after the injured captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to overpower the attacker. Another pilot travelling on board and a standby crew member helped regain control of the aircraft.All 182 people on board, including eight crew members, survived the incident.The incident has brought renewed attention to a question that aviation security measures introduced after 9/11 were not primarily designed to address: what happens when the threat comes from a member of the flight crew?Airlines have spent decades strengthening cockpit doors, tightening airport security and introducing procedures to prevent unauthorised access to aircraft. However, the Flydubai incident has raised concerns about pilot screening, the sharing of background information between countries, cockpit access and the industry's ability to respond when a member of the flight crew becomes violent.On October 8, airline executives acknowledged that preventing every such incident would be difficult, even as they defended existing safety standards. The incident is being investigated by authorities in the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, while Israel has indicated that it will review security arrangements for flights entering the country.How 9/11 changed aviation securityThe September 11, 2001, attacks fundamentally changed commercial aviation. Nineteen al-Qaeda hijackers took control of four passenger aircraft in the United States, crashing two into the World Trade Center in New York and one into the Pentagon. The fourth aircraft crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers resisted the hijackers. Nearly 3,000 people were killed.Before the attacks, airport security in the United States was largely handled by private contractors, cockpit access was less restrictive and passengers could carry certain items that would later be prohibited. The hijackers exploited these vulnerabilities to take control of the aircraft.The US government responded by creating the Transportation Security Administration in November 2001, tightening passenger and baggage screening, strengthening identity checks and expanding the federal air marshal programme.The most consequential change aboard aircraft was the introduction of reinforced, lockable cockpit doors designed to resist forced entry and firearms. US airlines were required to install reinforced doors by April 2003, with international aviation standards subsequently extending cockpit protection worldwide.Security procedures also expanded beyond passengers to include airport employees, restricted areas, baggage and cargo. Airlines and regulators developed additional safeguards to prevent aircraft from being seized by unauthorised individuals.These measures were designed primarily to prevent an external attacker from entering the flight deck and taking control of an aircraft. The Flydubai incident presents a different challenge: the alleged attacker was an authorised member of the flight crew who already had access to the cockpit.What happened aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073?On September 30, Flydubai flight FZ1073 was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 182 people on board when the co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain.The aircraft experienced a steep descent, losing around 16,000 feet in approximately 30 seconds. Flight-tracking data also showed the aircraft transmitting emergency signals during the incident.The injured captain reportedly managed to open the cockpit door, enabling passengers and crew members to overpower the co-pilot. Another pilot who was travelling on board subsequently helped regain control of the aircraft, which was diverted to Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia and landed safely.Reuters reported, citing Israeli officials familiar with the investigation, that the co-pilot had told interrogators in the UAE that he planned the attack before joining the airline. The allegation has not been established through a publicly announced court finding, and the UAE had not announced formal charges against him, according to Reuters' October 8 report.Israeli authorities have described the incident as a terrorist attack and an alleged attempt to crash the aircraft. Investigators are also examining how the suspect was cleared to serve on a flight bound for Israel.The incident's outcome has prompted questions about how much the response depended on circumstances that may not be present during another emergency.Saj Ahmad, chief analyst at aviation consultancy StrategicAero Research, told Al Jazeera that the presence of additional pilots aboard the aircraft was crucial.“It is frightening to think of what the outcome would have been if those additional pilots were not there to take control.”How secure is a cockpit door?Reinforced cockpit doors remain one of the central security measures introduced after 9/11. On modern commercial aircraft, the flight deck is protected by a reinforced door and an access-control system designed to prevent unauthorised entry.Under normal operating procedures, the door remains locked during flight. Cabin crew can request access, while an emergency-entry system provides a mechanism for authorised personnel to seek entry if a pilot does not respond. The system includes safeguards intended to prevent an attacker from simply entering the cockpit.However, these protections primarily address the threat of someone attempting to break into the flight deck from the cabin. They cannot, by themselves, prevent a violent confrontation between people already inside.Abhinav Singh, a pilot with a leading airline, told TOI that cockpit doors remain an essential security measure but cannot address every possible threat.“Reinforced cockpit doors and access-control systems were primarily strengthened after the September 11 attacks to prevent unauthorised access to the flight deck. They are an essential layer of aviation security, but no single security measure can address every possible threat, including one originating inside the cockpit itself,” he said.“If a pilot becomes violent, the situation is fundamentally different from an external intrusion because the person already has authorised access to the flight deck and may have control of the aircraft. The door can protect the cockpit from outside interference, but it cannot resolve a threat involving a person already inside,” he added.“Access-control procedures must therefore balance cockpit security with the need to manage emergencies. Any procedure for dealing with a violent crew member must account for the possibility that restricting access or delaying assistance could create additional risks. The broader objective should be to combine physical security with crew training, clear emergency procedures and effective coordination between the flight deck and cabin crew,” Singh said.The 2015 Germanwings crash exposed another dimension of the problem. Co-pilot Andreas Lubitz locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately flew the Airbus A320 into the French Alps, killing all 150 people on board.Following the crash, European aviation authorities recommended that two authorised people remain in the cockpit at all times. The recommendation was subsequently replaced by a more flexible, risk-based approach, allowing airlines to adopt safeguards suited to their operations.The Flydubai incident has renewed debate about whether existing access procedures adequately address situations in which one pilot attacks another, or whether additional measures could help the remaining crew regain control.Could pilot screening become stricter?The incident has also renewed scrutiny of how airlines recruit pilots and verify their professional and personal backgrounds.Pilots undergo licensing checks, medical assessments and background screening, but the process involves airlines, training institutions and regulators operating across different jurisdictions. A pilot may train in one country, obtain a licence in another and subsequently work for airlines based elsewhere.This can make it difficult to build a complete picture of an individual's professional history and identify relevant concerns when pilots move between employers.Abhinav Singh, a pilot with a leading airline, told TOI that airlines assess pilots through licensing checks, medical fitness assessments, training records and technical evaluations. However, verifying their complete employment and disciplinary histories across borders can be more complicated.“Pilot recruitment involves several layers of checks, including licence verification, medical fitness, training records, simulator assessments and technical evaluations. Airlines also examine a candidate’s flying experience and operational competence before allowing them to fly commercially. However, the depth of employment and background checks can vary depending on the airline, the regulatory framework and the country in which the pilot previously worked,” he said.“Verifying a pilot’s licence is relatively straightforward when the issuing authority and records are accessible. The more complicated part is establishing a complete picture of their previous employment, training history, performance and any disciplinary concerns across different jurisdictions. Records may be maintained by different regulators and operators, and information-sharing practices are not always uniform internationally,” he added.“This is why stronger cooperation between aviation regulators and standardised systems for verifying a pilot’s professional history are important. A licence establishes that a person meets specified requirements, but recruitment should also establish their professional record and continued fitness to operate safely,” Singh said.Following the Flydubai incident, Israel said it would strengthen security checks for pilots flying into the country. The investigation is expected to examine whether any concerns about the co-pilot had previously been raised and whether relevant information was shared with the authorities responsible for screening him.Investigators will need to establish whether existing safeguards were followed, whether relevant information was available to the airline and whether additional screening could realistically have prevented the incident.What happens if violence erupts in the cockpit?A violent confrontation between pilots creates a particularly difficult emergency because the people responsible for controlling the aircraft may themselves be involved.Singh told TOI that cabin crew can help manage security incidents and communicate with the flight deck, but their training and authority differ from those of a qualified pilot operating the aircraft.“The immediate priority in such a situation is to preserve control of the aircraft and prevent the confrontation from escalating. Commercial aviation procedures are designed around clear responsibilities, communication and the management of abnormal situations. However, a violent confrontation inside the cockpit creates an exceptionally difficult scenario because the people responsible for flying the aircraft may themselves be involved in the emergency,” he said.“Cabin crew are trained to manage security incidents and communicate with the flight deck, but their training and authority are not equivalent to those of a qualified pilot operating the aircraft. Their role would depend on the circumstances, the aircraft’s procedures and the extent to which communication with the flight deck remains possible,” he added.“An appropriately qualified pilot travelling as a passenger could potentially provide assistance, depending on the circumstances and airline procedures. However, it would be unsafe to assume that any available person could simply take over. This is why emergency preparedness, crew resource management and clear escalation procedures matter. Airlines and regulators need to examine whether existing training adequately addresses situations involving violence between flight crew members, rather than focusing exclusively on external security threats,” Singh said.The presence of another pilot aboard the Flydubai flight may have helped avert a worse outcome, but the incident has raised questions about how airlines prepare crews for emergencies involving a member of the flight deck team.Does aviation need another security overhaul?The Flydubai incident does not, by itself, establish that the aviation industry's existing safeguards are inadequate. Nor does it demonstrate that any single additional screening measure would have prevented the attack.It does, however, expose a vulnerability that differs from the one aviation authorities sought to address after 9/11. The earlier reforms focused on preventing unauthorised individuals from entering the cockpit and using aircraft as weapons. The latest incident raises questions about how to respond when a person with legitimate access becomes the threat.Singh told TOI that the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and national regulators should examine cross-border employment verification, confidential reporting of safety concerns, crew conflict management and recurrent training.“Incidents involving violence or deliberate actions by flight crew highlight the need to continuously reassess aviation safety measures. The Germanwings crash demonstrated the catastrophic consequences of a pilot deliberately causing an aircraft to crash, while reports of violence involving crew members raise questions about how airlines identify, prevent and respond to threats originating within the operating crew.“The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and national regulators should examine whether existing standards provide sufficient guidance on cross-border employment verification, confidential reporting of safety concerns, crew conflict management and responses to deliberate acts of violence. There should also be greater consistency in how airlines assess previous employment records and verify qualifications across jurisdictions.“Another area for review is recurrent training. Pilots and cabin crew should be prepared to recognise and respond to serious onboard security incidents, including scenarios involving a member of the flight crew. Such training must be realistic, proportionate and designed around preserving aircraft control.“However, additional security restrictions alone will not solve the problem. Regulators need to strike a balance between safeguarding cockpit security, protecting the wellbeing and rights of aviation professionals, and ensuring that credible safety concerns can be reported without fear of retaliation. The ultimate objective should be a system that identifies risks early, responds effectively when incidents occur and learns from every serious event.”Airline executives have also cautioned that no safety system can eliminate every risk posed by an individual acting deliberately.Ryanair Group chief executive Michael O'Leary, speaking at an Airlines for Europe press conference in Brussels on October 8, said: “If you have somebody who is a mad person in a cockpit, it's very difficult to legislate for it,”Lufthansa chief executive Carsten Spohr also stressed the limits of preventive measures while defending the industry's safety standards.“We have to face the fact that there is no absolute safety and security in this industry,” Spohr said.The remarks reflect the challenge facing airlines and regulators: strengthening safeguards without creating procedures that introduce new vulnerabilities or discourage pilots from reporting health and personal difficulties.The Germanwings crash prompted greater attention to pilots' mental health, including psychological assessments and support systems. However, mental health screening and security screening address different risks. Experiencing depression, anxiety or stress does not, by itself, indicate that someone poses a security threat. A system that makes pilots reluctant to disclose health problems could undermine safety by discouraging them from seeking help.Possible areas for review include the exchange of pilot background information across national borders, verification of professional histories when pilots change employers, crew security checks and procedures for responding to violence in the flight deck. Authorities may also examine cockpit access arrangements, emergency communications and recurrent crew training.Any changes will need to be based on evidence gathered during the investigation rather than a reaction to an extraordinary incident. Aviation safety depends on multiple layers of protection, from recruitment and training to cockpit procedures and emergency response.The challenge for regulators is to identify where those layers failed, if they did, and determine whether existing rules were properly implemented before introducing new requirements.Twenty-five years after 9/11 transformed aviation security, the Flydubai incident has raised a different question for the industry: how can it protect an aircraft when the person posing the threat is already inside the cockpit?You use AI every day. articles.title: New Forest wildfire cost estimated at £600,000
articles.summary: Tackling the blaze required around 5,500 hours of firefighter time, a finance director says.
articles.body:
A record-breaking wildfire in a national park is estimated to have cost a fire service £600,000.

More than 1 sq km (247 acres) of the New Forest was destroyed after the fire spread from a blazing van on 9 August.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority said the incident was the largest in the brigade's history.

Chief financial officer Rob Sarfas told a fire authority meeting the blaze required around 5,500 hours of firefighter time.

He said: "We think the number is approximately £600,000 for that incident, in terms of additional cost."

The fire closed the A31 - a major tourist and commuter route between Hampshire and Dorset - for nearly two weeks.

It came during an exceptionally busy summer for firefighters, the authority heard.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight crews dealt with around 1,400 outdoor fires in July and August, including 75 classified as wildfires, a 52% increase on the same period last year.

The service had been forecasting a £1.2m underspend at the end of the first quarter of the financial year, before the cost of the summer response became clear.

The authority has asked the government to help cover some of the cost of responding to the wildfire, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, which is responsible for fire services, previously said it would ensure fire services have the resources they need.

A spokesperson said: "This includes making almost £1.95bn available for fire services in England, and investing nearly £100m in the biggest upgrade to national resilience in almost 20 years."

articles.title: Mexican judge sentences three men for murders of Australian, US surfers
articles.summary: The trial in Baja California had revealed chilling details of the triple homicide of the surfers.
articles.body:
A Mexican judge found three men guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.

The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded Friday after Judge Raul Hernandez in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesus Gerardo Garcia, alias “El Kekas”, Irineo Francisco “N,” and Angel Jesus “N” were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and American Carter Redd Rhoad, 30.

The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking.

“Today’s guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons, Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad, whose lives were so cruelly taken from them in 2024,” said father Martin Robinson.

The three travelled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf and camped near the coastal city of Ensenada, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 80 kilometres (50 miles) from Ensenada, they were reported missing. Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well, all with gunshot wounds to their heads.

Garcia, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Francisco, and Jesus.

During the monthlong trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that Garcia confessed to her that he arrived at the tent where the foreigners were staying with a 9mm pistol.

Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them, and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said.

She said Garcia had bragged about “how beautifully” the victims cried and about items he robbed from them.

The state prosecutor’s office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and “instigated one of her companions to rob them”, which they did the following day.

The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims’ cellphones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to “aggravated robbery with violence” and “vehicle theft with violence” in an expedited proceeding. However, Garcia and his two accomplices decided to go to trial.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists.

The judge will announce the final sentence on October 16. The Baja California State Attorney General’s Office requested for each defendant the “exemplary sentence” of 210 years in prison.

“No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honoring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were,” said Martin Robinson. “They will never be forgotten.”

articles.title: Wildfires came 'worryingly' close to our animal rescue centre
articles.summary: International Animal Rescue says its Borneo conservation project has been impacted by Indonesian fires.
articles.body:
A charity has described how wildfires came "worryingly" close to its rescue centre.

International Animal Rescue, based in East Sussex, told the BBC its conservation project in Borneo has been impacted by wildfires sweeping across Indonesia.

"When the fires really got a grip, they came worryingly close to our rescue centre - literally within a few hundred metres," said the charity's chief executive Gavin Bruce.

"The team there has just done the most remarkable effort," he said, adding that animals had been moved to keep them safe.

Wildfires have been burning throughout parts of Indonesia for weeks, sending smoke across the country and into neighbouring Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.

International Animal Rescue said it was also having to rescue orangutans from the fires, with 46 of the critically endangered animal moved to safety so far.

Dr Kamale Sanchez, who works for the charity in Indonesia, told the BBC she was sleeping deep within the forests to rescue more.

She said forest fires in the area "have got even more out of control".

"We are experiencing a very hot season," said Sanchez, explaining that it was about five to six degrees above normal temperatures for the time of year.

This year's wildfire season has been called one of Indonesia's worst in years .

It is primarily caused by illegal slash-and-burn practices used by farmers and companies as a cheap method to clear vegetation, though experts say the "super" El Niño this year has exacerbated drought conditions.

Human activities, such as the burning of fossil fuels, are driving climate change that is making extreme weather events more common and intense , say scientists.

articles.title: With or without Hamas
articles.summary: Hamas’s fate will not profoundly shape Gaza’s future.
articles.body:
As we begin the fourth year of a war that has brought the near-total destruction of Gaza, calls for Hamas to surrender administrative authority and evacuate the Strip are intensifying. For Gaza to have any viable future, it is argued, the group’s political and military wings must be dismantled.

While Hamas’s fate is a critical question, charting a meaningful path towards recovery is impossible without addressing the realities that gave rise to it in the first place.

What is happening today in Gaza is directly related to the origins of the Palestinian-Israeli question, which has little to do with any particular armed group.

Hamas did not exist in 1948, when hundreds of Palestinian villages, including Naj and Huj, were depopulated and destroyed during the Nakba – the Palestinian catastrophe that accompanied the creation of the State of Israel – to make way for the establishment of Sderot, Or HaNer and numerous other Israeli cities and villages built upon their ruins.

The group had not yet been established in 1967, when the Arab-Israeli War took place and Israel initiated its military occupation of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, while simultaneously seizing and unilaterally annexing East Jerusalem—actions that actively set the stage for the broader Israeli settlement project.

In the following decades, the occupation profoundly affected Palestinian society. That, combined with growing religious influence—as the number of local mosques tripled from 200 to 600 between 1967 and 1987 — and a vacuum left behind by a fading secular nationalist leadership, prepared the ground for the rise of faith-based nationalist factions. The outbreak of the First Intifada in 1987 was a political turning point that directly triggered the creation of Hamas.

The group was established by a group of Palestinian men, including three prominent figures. Ibrahim al-Yazouri, was born in Bait Daras, near today’s Ashdod, and was just eight years old when soldiers of the Haganah killed members of his family and expelled the survivors to Khan Younis, south of Gaza City.

Another founder, Abdulaziz al-Rantisi, was born in Yibna—a village near Jaffa whose ruins now sit beneath the Israeli city of Yavne. He was only a year old when Israeli forces expelled his family to Khan Younis.

Lastly, Ahmed Yassin, was born in al-Jura, a village near Ashkelon that was razed to the ground by the Israeli military. He was 12 years old, when he and his family had to flee their home and settle in al-Shati refugee camp on the Gaza coast.

Highlighting this history should not be misunderstood as an attempt to downplay Hamas’s responsibilities. However, the group’s actions cannot be separated from the historical context and the role the State of Israel has played throughout this process.

Unlike the self-proclaimed ISIL (ISIS) and other groups that have emerged in recent years—which lack deep roots in local societies and rely on obsolete ideologies—Palestinian factions are deeply intertwined with local society and national identity.

While Hamas’s trajectory is marked by several disastrous decisions—most notably its fatal decision to launch the assault on Israel on October 7, 2023—the group remains, above all, a symptom of a century of suffering, oppression and a relentless struggle for self-determination.

Any proposed solution – with or without Hamas – to the war in Gaza that fails to address these underlying realities is bound to fail. It must be emphasised here that the widespread tendency in the West to frame the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination as a “reward for Hamas” is deeply flawed. It stems from a systemic prejudice that must not be normalised.

The right was enshrined in international law and supported by an overwhelming majority of nations long before Hamas’s attack.

It is also a mistake to equate Hamas’s actions with the will of the Palestinian people. Today, nearly 50 percent of the population of the Gaza Strip is under the age of 18; when Hamas won the elections in 2006, more than half of Gaza’s current residents had not even been born.

Furthermore, in an Arab Barometer survey conducted in the West Bank and Gaza between late September and early October 2023, only 29 percent of Gaza respondents said they trusted the Hamas-led government. The majority blamed poverty on internal factors; 31 percent directly pointed to the Hamas authorities as being responsible for the situation.

Crucially, a majority (54 percent) supported a two-state solution to the conflict; 73 percent favoured a peaceful resolution. Just 20 percent favoured military action.

The presence of Hamas in Gaza cannot justify the Strip’s wholesale destruction and the crimes committed against civilians that have resulted in Israeli officials facing accusations of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Hamas was not present at al-Nasr Hospital in November 2023, when the Israeli army left newborns to die in incubators after forcing their caregivers to evacuate and prevented their return. Hamas was not in the car with Hind Rajab, the young Palestinian girl, when Israeli forces fired 335 bullets into it in January 2024.

Ironically and unsurprisingly, Hamas has long been viewed as useful by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to maintain the argument that there are no moderate Palestinian partners with whom to negotiate.

This strategy aligns closely with the 2017 Subjugation Plan—officially titled “Israel’s Decisive Plan”—a political and ideological framework presented by Israeli far-right politician Bezalel Smotrich in 2017, which explicitly advocated for disregarding Palestinian national aspirations.

This refusal to address the structural roots has frozen the contemporary diplomatic landscape. The Israeli unwillingness to engage in dialogue with Palestinian interlocutors contrasts sharply with the pragmatic realism historically articulated by Israeli General Moshe Dayan, who famously observed that peacemaking requires negotiating with enemies rather than friends.

Today’s diplomatic landscape is defined by a deep imbalance in expectations. For many years, Palestinian factions have faced strict, non-negotiable prerequisites to attain international political legitimacy—such as the explicit recognition of Israel, the renunciation of violence and adherence to past accords.

Conversely, no reciprocal demands have been placed on Israeli authorities, who face no requirement to recognise a sovereign Palestinian state, honour previous treaties, or renounce violence.

In fact, Israel’s own political evolution is intertwined with factions that utilised political violence. Paramilitary organisations such as the Irgun, led by Menachem Begin, and the Lehi, led by Yitzhak Shamir, conducted operations that targeted civilians, yet both leaders eventually transitioned into mainstream politics and became prime ministers.

This power imbalance directly manifests as a diplomatic asymmetry also in recent ceasefire negotiations, which remain deadlocked by Israel’s demand for the complete disarmament of Hamas. By establishing the eradication of the group’s military capabilities as a precondition for a permanent truce, Israel’s leadership sets a political threshold that effectively forecloses a negotiated settlement.

This allows the Israeli government to perpetuate a status quo that yields significant strategic, territorial and political dividends.

Ultimately, doing away with Hamas will not do away with the Palestinian demand for freedom, nor will it satisfy Israel’s and Palestine’s legitimate right to security. The conflict did not begin with the rise of a militant faction and it will never end until all involved parties finally realise that, as Peruvian Indigenous jurist Dionisio Inca Yupanqui warned two centuries ago, “a nation that oppresses another ultimately forges its own chains”.

articles.title: A 112-year-old San Francisco home beside the Presidio sold for $15 million just two weeks after listing at $7.999 million; nine competing offers pushed the 4,490-square-foot property nearly 88% above the asking price
articles.summary: The house at 2 Sixth Avenue in San Francisco went on the market on September 17 at $7.999 million.
articles.body: The house at 2 Sixth Avenue in San Francisco went on the market on September 17 at $7.999 million. Three weeks later, something rare happened in the real estate market. The house sold for a whopping $15 million, which is 87.5% above the asking price, the New York Post reported.Built in 1914, the 4,490-square-foot home remained in the original owner’s possession for 70 years before being sold for the first time in 1984, according to The Independent.The buyer has not been publicly identified. The listing agent, Maureen Terris of Compass, described the property as a ‘once-in-a-generation listing’. Ronda Priestner, also of Compass, represented the buyer.A house at the edge of the PresidioThe house sits on a 9,233-square-foot lot that borders Presidio National Park. The listing describes the property as a “rare convergence of architecture, landscape, and place – a private retreat”. Most San Francisco houses are wedged shoulder to shoulder with their neighbours. But this one is fully detached and set back from the street. “This house featured well-preserved architectural elements from 1914, was fully detached and set back from the street, and was situated on an oversized lot with front and back gardens bordering the Presidio National Park,” Terris told the Post.“The residence is a beautiful expression of San Francisco’s First Bay Tradition,” the listing says.Inside the 112-year-old houseThe house spans 4,490 square feet, with four bedrooms and three bathrooms. It has original redwood trim, a coffered dining room ceiling and fireplaces in the living room and dining room, along with a butler’s pantry that provides generous workspace and storage. The redwood staircase leads to the four bedrooms on the upper level. The primary suite is spacious and comes with a bathroom, three closets and a dressing room. The dining room has French doors that open onto a terrace. The library looks out over the Presidio. The kitchen has a range set into a brick wall.“Mature front and rear gardens envelop the property in greenery, while verdant outlooks extend into the Presidio and golf course. Windows, French doors, terraces and direct garden access blur the boundary between indoors and out,” the listing says. The French doors open onto the private patio. There is also a beautiful garden at the back. The house also comes with a spacious side-by-side two-car garage and more than five driveway spaces.Listed at nearly $8 million, sold for $15 millionIn September, the house went on the market for $7.999 million. There were many prospective buyers. “We received nine strong offers,” Terris told the outlet. In less than a month, the sale closed at $15 million, which is 87.5% above the asking price. At $15 million, the sale works out to about $3,341 per square foot. The sellers were Bob and Joan McGrath, according to SFGATE. Bob McGrath founded McGrath RentCorp. The couple are in their 90s and ready to move on, Terris told the paper.The city’s housing market is quite unique, with many buyers willing to pay well above asking prices. “Much of the wealth generation, especially around real estate, as a result of the AI companies is actually already in the system,” Mike Simonsen, chief economist at real estate firm Compass, told The Independent. “These are people who have already moved into town with big salaries and go, ‘I’ll take whatever apartment is available.’”Interestingly, this sale wasn’t a record for the city, as a house in Cow Hollow sold in May for 88.7% above the asking price, also for about $15 million. Bids a million dollars or more above asking are becoming ordinary here, and a house that sells this fast tends to stand out only for how much it went for.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Man dies after entering tiger enclosure at UK wildlife park, police say
articles.summary: A man was seriously injured after jumping into a tiger enclosure at a UK wildlife park, police say.
articles.body: A man has died after suffering serious injuries when he entered into a tiger enclosure at a UK wildlife park, South Yorkshire Police said. A police statement said: “At 1.35pm today (Saturday 10 October) we received reports of a man entering a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.” “Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene,” police said. The tiger was uninjured in the incident, the police said. The police added that the man’s family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. “Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time.” The park was evacuated following the incident. The tiger remained in the enclosure following the attack, and there is no wider risk posed to the public, according to authorities. The police spokesperson added that people are being encouraged not to share “distressing” footage circulating online of the man being mauled by the tiger. Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near the city of Doncaster in northern England, confirmed in a statement that a “serious incident” took place at one of its tiger enclosures and the park’s emergency response procedures were “immediately activated.” The park announced it would be shut for the rest of Saturday and Sunday. This story has been updated.

articles.title: Christa Pike, who survived an execution attempt, is discharged from hospital, attorney says
articles.summary: Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison, according to a statement released by her attorneys.
articles.body: NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison, according to a statement released by her attorneys. Pike, 50, was discharged from the hospital and is back at the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years, her attorneys said in a statement. “She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” her attorneys said in a statement released Saturday. Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her by lethal injection on Sept. 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike had been in a hospital since the failed execution. The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.

articles.title: Multiple people wounded in attack on Riyadh airport, Saudi aviation authority says
articles.summary: Many people were wounded in a blast at Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday, according to two eyewitnesses and two people briefed on the matter, and travellers were evacuated from parts of the facility.
articles.body: Several people were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh on Saturday that forced a suspension of operations, the country’s civil aviation authority said. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, but it comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis against Saudi Arabia. The airport had already been struck in two earlier attacks this week that left four people dead and exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s ability to defend itself as it wages war on the Houthis. Saudi Arabia’s early warning system did not issue an alert ahead of Saturday’s incident. The Saudi government’s media office did not immediately respond to questions from Reuters. One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing toward the facility. An injured traveler told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed. Following the attack, US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether the United States planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. “We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said. The US Embassy in Riyadh said it was “aware of attacks” and “strongly recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas.” The UK and Irish embassies in Saudi Arabia said in statements on X that they were also aware of a “serious incident” at the airport. The Canadian embassy said that “ongoing military activity” had impacted operations at the airport. Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or canceled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point. Kuwait Airways said it had canceled flights to and from the Saudi capital due to what it described as the closure of Riyadh airport because of the “security situation” there. Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways earlier canceled multiple flights between their respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences. Organizers of those conferences said on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, and they sought to reassure attendees of their security. The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group earlier this month. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Hurricane Isaias leaves two dead and 800,000 without power in US Southeast
articles.summary: Storm damage stretches across Florida and Alabama as officials warn of continued flooding and possible tornadoes.
articles.body:
Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, has killed two people and left hundreds of thousands of customers without power across the southeastern United States.

The storm made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane before weakening as it moved inland through Alabama overnight.

One person died in Birmingham, Alabama, when a tree fell on a house overnight, according to local emergency officials. A second person was killed in Escambia County, Florida, after a tree fell during the storm, according to local authorities.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said on Saturday that state officials had not confirmed any storm-related fatalities, including the report from Escambia County.

Isaias hit land with sustained winds of 169km/h (105mph), bringing powerful gusts and heavy rain to the Florida Panhandle. By Saturday morning, the storm had weakened to a post-tropical cyclone with wind speeds of about 55km/h (35mph).

More than 900,000 electricity customers in Florida, Alabama and Georgia were without power early Saturday morning. That number has since gone down to under 800,000, according to PowerOutage.us.

Fallen trees and downed power lines caused widespread disruption, while flooding forced road closures in parts of southern Alabama, including Houston County. Alabama Governor Kay Ivey said on Saturday morning that her team was concerned about “strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes”.

Local officials in Pensacola, Florida reported strong winds that damaged an airport and tore the roof off a hotel. Trees and power lines also came down across the city, leaving some residents without electricity and roads blocked.

Despite the storm’s weakening, officials warned that dangerous conditions could persist. Heavy rainfall threatened flash flooding across parts of the Southeast.

“The flooding story is not over,” DeSantis said on Saturday, warning that saturated ground and continued rainfall could cause dangerous flooding a day or two after the storm passed. He said state search and rescue resources would remain available in case rapidly rising waters required emergency rescues.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned residents to be alert for contractors seeking to exploit storm victims as homeowners begin repairing damaged properties.

articles.title: Inside Hasan Piker’s radical views on America, Israel and socialism
articles.summary: Hasan Piker's critics claimed his Marxist worldview goes beyond progressivism, casting America as fundamentally corrupt and worse than al-Qaeda.
articles.body: Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has built his online brand through intense commentary on political topics ranging from economics to foreign policy. During his daily streams, which last several hours, he gives his takes on the issues of the day, often through a combative left-wing lens. As Piker's influence has moved from his online audience and into the real world, including Democratic politics and campus events, critics argue his ideology deserves more scrutiny. To his supporters, Piker is an effective messenger for a generation looking for something outside traditional political structures. However, multiple critics who spoke with Fox News Digital described the streamer's worldview as going beyond typical progressive and anti-establishment outlooks. They claim his beliefs cast America as fundamentally corrupt, treat socialism as the answer to economic frustrations and frame Israel as uniquely immoral and illegitimate. WHO IS HASAN PIKER? MEET THE FAR-LEFT STREAMER WHO IS STIRRING UP CONTROVERSY AND DIVIDING DEMOCRATS Eli Lake, a senior reporter at The Free Press and host of the podcast "Breaking History," told Fox News Digital that Piker's belief system is "informed in many ways by a Marxist view of history" and that the streamer is part of "a tradition of the anti-American left." "There is a tradition of elements of the Left that believes that the country and the republic are rotten to its core, and I think that that is a distinction from, you know, a more kind of hopeful version of progressivism," Lake told Fox News Digital. Lake contrasted Piker's beliefs with a reform-minded view in which the Declaration of Independence serves as a starting point from which the U.S. would progress. The goal, according to Lake, would be to hold the country to its stated ideals, an approach that he said is "distinct from the way that Hasan Piker understands the United States as sort of irredeemably evil." In one of Piker's more recent controversial statements, the streamer said in an interview with Axios that the U.S. was worse than al-Qaeda. "Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes," Piker told Axios. "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world." Lake criticized Piker's remarks in an article for The Free Press, writing that the streamer's inability to "to grasp the distinction between intentionally and unintentionally killing civilians" showed his "moral illiteracy." HASAN PIKER ADMITS HE HAS 'DIALED DOWN' HIS OPINIONS AFTER PUBLIC AND DEMOCRATIC BACKLASH "I almost felt guilty writing a column because I could assume it was so obvious that America is nothing like al-Qaeda. Al-Qaeda deliberately is trying to kill as many civilians as it can," Lake told Fox News Digital. "If Hasan Piker cannot distinguish between America and its foreign policy and that of al-Qaeda in a moral sense at least, or he thinks they're equal or 'pound for pound' America is worse, then he's helpless." Piker's critics argue that his moral framework also shapes his views of Israel. They say that he goes beyond criticizing the Israeli government or its policies and frames the Jewish state's existence as being up for debate, something that Tanya Tsikanovsky, a first-generation American whose parents fled the Soviet Union, takes issue with. "I think that we can sit here and discuss the government of Israel, but we're not citizens of Israel. Certainly Hasan Piker is not, and we don't live there," Tsikanovsky told Fox News Digital. "As a Zionist, and as someone who is a proud jew, I'm here to care about the existence of the state. I just want it to exist." She also pointed out that Piker does not apply the same standards he has for Israel to other countries. "You know we don't spend our time debating the existence of any other country. Like Hasan's not saying, 'Maybe Switzerland shouldn't really be a country.' No, like, we're good with every other country," she said, adding that, in her view, the reason for this singling out of Israel is antisemitism. Tsikanovsky told Fox News Digital that her immigrant parents view the country in an entirely different light from Piker. She said that they see the U.S. as a place where they were finally able to be free and live as equals. "My parents came here from the USSR, and they kiss the ground of this country because we know that it's the best country on Earth," she said. "There really is no other place in the world that provides the same level of freedom, and Hassan Piker is using that freedom specifically to get everyone to want to lose it and without even realizing it." She argued that Piker's worldview is hostile to the American system and that it welcomes the exact things that families like hers fled. FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER DEFENDS HIMSELF FROM ANTISEMITISM ACCUSATIONS IN INTERVIEW WITH JEWISH OUTLET "[Piker] is aligning himself with an ideology that will embrace Sharia law, that will embrace communism," she said. Piker's critics say his worldview is not merely defined by what he opposes, but also the economic system he promotes. Venezuelan-born economist Daniel Di Martino argued that there is a hidden danger to Piker's economic stances, mainly the appeal of socialist promises to young people frustrated with capitalism. Di Martino, who grew up in Venezuela before immigrating to the U.S., said that socialism was more than an abstract idea, it was a system that made ordinary life substantially worse. He described growing up under socialism as "feeling the constant deterioration of my quality of life in even the daily smallest things." Recently, Piker took the 12 Axes political test on one of his daily streams, and the results showed that he was closely aligned economically with late Venezuelan socialist leader Hugo Chávez, something Di Martino saw as a significant red flag. "Their economic policies are not those of Norway and Denmark. They're the ones of Venezuela. They are the ones that destroy the country I come from," Di Martino said. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA BACKS 'OUR TWITCH STREAMER' HASAN PIKER, RIPS ANTI-SOCIALISM HOUSE RESOLUTION He recalled Venezuela unraveling before his eyes as the government began using state resources to provide free goods and services. When oil money was no longer enough, Di Martino said, the government printed money, fueling inflation. Eventually, shortages came and Di Martino recalled the government blaming business owners for being greedy and claiming that citizens were hoarding food. "They hailed bread lines and shortages as evidence that there was so much demand because Venezuelans were so well off. I mean, imagine how laughable these arguments [were]," Di Martino told Fox News Digital. "And eventually they said that inflation was imaginary, it was all made up in our heads. And then we had no electricity, and then we have no water," he added. "And then crime went up and it went unpunished. And then they jailed their political opponents when they tried to speak up, and then they rigged the elections because that is the only way for socialists to stay in power, because it always fails, so they have to rig the elections to stay in power." For Di Martino, the real danger of Piker's growing influence is not simply that he has a large online audience, but that his ideas are moving into Democratic politics and could eventually shape U.S. government policy. "Even though he's not running, the people running on the socialist side, the democratic socialist candidates, listen to him and have his ideas, which are Marxist-Leninist ideas, are the ideas of the Chinese Communist Party — which is why he goes there — are the ideas of the socialist party of Venezuela, of the communist party of Cuba. That is what these people stand for," Di Martino said. "And so, we should be worried, not because Hassan Piker is popular, he is not, we should be worried because his ideas are gonna make it to the Congress and to the state and local governments." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Piker's critics are not merely concerned with the provocative things he says regularly online, but that his platform is reaching a group of voters that the left has tried to court. In their eyes, this could mean the adoption of hard-left politics in the government, putting the very idea of the American system at risk. Fox News Digital reached out to Piker for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title: Eritrea urges UN to intervene in standoff with Ethiopia
articles.summary: The neighbouring countries blame one another for starting war amid heightened tensions and fears of a wider conflict.
articles.body:
Eritrea has asked the United Nations to take “deterrent measures” after what it called Ethiopia’s “declaration of war” in the conflict over the Tigray region.

Eritrea’s request comes a day after Addis Ababa, in a letter to the Security Council, accused Asmara of launching an “all-out invasion”, saying Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 kilometres (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s Tigray.

In a separate letter to the council on Saturday, Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh said the claims of an Eritrean incursion were part of an Ethiopian plan to justify a war of aggression and urged the UN to intervene, invoking Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which allows measures from sanctions to military action.

The neighbouring countries have accused each other of starting a war over Tigray, where Ethiopia says Eritrea is backing rebels.

An alliance of seven armed groups launched attacks against federal Ethiopian forces in the northern region last month, as they attempt to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.

Eritrean forces have since reportedly intruded into Ethiopian territory, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of backing the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).

The Ethiopian army pushed TPLF rebels back this week and seized the region’s capital, Mekelle. It also said it launched drone strikes against Eritrean troops in the region.

“Eritrea requests the UN Security Council to forcefully condemn Ethiopia’s deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea … and take the requisite deterrent measures,” Eritrea’s Saleh said in the letter on Saturday.

He said Ethiopia’s action would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.

Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos on Friday accused Eritrea of “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.

Timothewos invoked Ethiopia’s right to self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter, but he did not specify what measures the country was taking.

Faisal Roble, a Horn of Africa specialist, believes both sides are “preparing for the last phase of an open conflict”.

“There is really no doubt that both of them are inching towards an open conflict,” he told Al Jazeera from the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.

“Whatever they write to the United Nations, it is just posturing and making sure that they have some sort of international support on their side,” the analyst added.

In his letter, Saleh called Ethiopia’s actions “deceitful attempts to rationalise its brazen acts of war”, claiming that they were “hollow in substance”.

Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accused Ethiopia on Friday of pursuing aggression against Eritrea through its demands for sovereign access to the Red Sea. Writing on X, he did not explicitly confirm or deny the reported troop crossings.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.

Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, and they fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000.

Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years.

Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly insisted that it has a right to direct sea access, which Eritrea interprets as a threat to invade and seize its port at Assab.

TPLF fighters battled Ethiopian government forces, then backed by Eritrea, in a devastating 2020-2022 war.

articles.title: In 1916, Florida’s USDA plant station tested Burma reed for erosion control and gardens; it escaped cultivation and is now listed as a Florida noxious weed
articles.summary: Discover the journey of Burma reed, once tested for erosion control by the USDA, now classified as a noxious weed in Florida. Learn how this invasive grass has impacted South Florida's pine rocklands and the measures taken to control its spread.
articles.body: Burma reed was once tested by the U.S. Department of Agriculture in Florida for erosion control and ornamental use, and is now listed as a noxious weed in the state. The grass had invaded nearly 75% of Miami-Dade County's pine rocklands outside Everglades National Park by 1993, according to the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services.The plant is scientifically known as Neyraudia reynaudiana, and is native to warm regions of Asia, including parts of India, Nepal, Taiwan and Indonesia. It is a perennial grass that can grow as tall as 15 feet and form dense clumps, and its flowering stalks can carry large, feathery plumes.It was tested as a useful plantThe USDA introduced Burma reed to its Plant Introduction Station in Coconut Grove in the early 20th century, and Florida's agriculture department says that the plant was introduced there in 1916 as a potential erosion-control and ornamental species, following which it was subsequently planted at the Florida Botanical Garden and Arboretum. Burma reed tolerates a range of soil, light and moisture conditions, and it can grow particularly well in infertile, rocky, dry locations that are exposed to full sun, according to the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services.The grass produces large quantities of seeds that are dispersed by wind, while pieces of its underground rhizomes can produce new plants. Florida officials say fragmented rhizomes can be moved by construction equipment and limestone quarrying, and that combination matters in disturbed areas, where soil and plant material are frequently moved. Removing individual plants does not prevent the grass from returning once they become established, because the underground rhizomes can survive.It spread through South Florida's pine rocklandsBurma reed had invaded nearly 75% of the pine rocklands in Miami-Dade County outside Everglades National Park by 1993, according to FDACS, with the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences also classifying Burma reed as a Category I invasive species in Florida. Pine rocklands are one of the habitats affected most heavily by the grass, and UF/IFAS says Burma reed can form dense, nearly single-species stands in these ecosystems, which crowd out native plants. The plant also produces substantial leaf litter and can alter the local fire regime. The grass can reach 10 to 15 feet in height, depending on conditions; its stems grow from short, coarse rhizomes, and mature clumps can contain numerous stalks. Florida officials say it flowers throughout the year and produces seeds that can be carried by wind.Florida now treats it as a noxious weedBurma reed is now listed on Florida's Noxious Weed List, and UF/IFAS classifies it as prohibited for use in the state, with its distribution remaining concentrated mainly in South Florida, including Miami-Dade, Broward, Monroe and Collier counties. The USDA Forest Service describes silkreed, which is another common name for Burma reed, as an invasive nonnative grass in Florida. Its review says that the plant can establish first in disturbed sites and later spread into less disturbed habitats. It has been documented along roads, in vacant lots, on limestone spoil piles and in several native plant communities.Burma reed's above-ground growth can be killed by fire, but the plants can resprout from their rhizomes, and UF/IFAS notes that the species can respond quickly after burning, sometimes growing before many native plants have recovered. Florida now restricts the plant that was once tested for erosion control and ornamental use, and state guidance recommends preventing its spread and controlling established populations before they expand into additional habitat.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pope Leo decries death penalty as Hegseth’s public execution plan sparks backlash
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV on Saturday called capital punishment “inadmissible” on World Day Against the Death Penalty, amid the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the December execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan in Texas. “The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” the pontiff wrote on…
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV on Saturday called capital punishment “inadmissible” on World Day Against the Death Penalty, amid the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the December execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan in Texas.

“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” the pontiff wrote on social media .

“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption,” he continued.

On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the public would be able to view the convicted terrorist’s Dec. 3 execution by firing squad. Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted in the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, which killed 13 people and injured 32 others.

While the pontiff did not directly comment on Hasan’s case, other Catholic leaders and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle denounced the livestream plans directly.

Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin told reporters Friday that the plans were unacceptable, according to The Vatican News.

“It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this method in this day and age,” he said. “I do not know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle. However guilty the person may be, there are other ways.”

The president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, Archbishop Paul Croakley, urged the Pentagon to reconsider the public execution.

“In no way can Hassan’s actions be condoned, but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” he said in an interview with Vatican News.

The Pentagon declined to comment on the pontiff’s criticism.

articles.title: Nine killed in shooting in US state of Pennsylvania, including two children
articles.summary: The shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania happened on Friday, according to state officials. The attacker is among the dead.
articles.body:
Nine people were killed Friday in a shooting in the US state of Pennsylvania, according to Governor Josh Shapiro. Police said the suspected shooter was among the nine dead.

Local media reported that two children were also among those killed at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, which is 188 kilometres (117 miles) north of Pittsburgh.

Police in the city of Erie were called Friday around 5:00pm local time (21:00 GMT) to reports of shots fired and discovered two women dead in the street, the Erie News Now outlet said.

The attacker barricaded himself inside the home as police surrounded the building and ordered him to exit.

More gunshots were heard during the standoff, Erie News Now reported.

When police eventually entered the building, they found several more victims around the home, including the two children. The deceased attacker had an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, the outlet said, citing police.

Erie News Now said that police officers who responded to the scene were being offered counselling over the horrifying incident.

“I have not seen anything like this in my 28-plus years,” Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah told a local news station on Saturday. “I’m not sure that the city of Erie has ever seen the loss of life and the devastation that we just witnessed.”

Lorah declined to provide more details but said the circumstances of the shooting were “deeply disturbing”.

Shapiro said Saturday he offered his administration’s “full support” to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin.

Mass shootings occur frequently in the United States, where guns vastly outnumber the population and efforts to increase firearm restrictions face steep political and legal hurdles.
